Skills: learned and developed abilities. A Skill starts at the value of its associated Characteristic (shown on the Character Sheet and/ or the entry for the relevant Skill in Chapter 4, page 110). Each Advance increases it by +5. Your starting Skills come from your Species and Career. There are three types of Skill: Basic Skills can be used by anyone, even without any Advances.

Advanced Skills can only be used if you have at least one Advance in the Skill.

Grouped Skills cover broad areas. When you take an Advance, choose a specialization such as Lore (Empire) or Lore (Tilea).

Armour: record your Armour (page 307) here, and write the total Armour Points (APs) in the Armour diagram on the front of the sheet.

Corruption and Mutation: exposure to Chaos leads to Corruption and Mutation (page 187), but your Character begins the game without such curses.

Trappings, Encumbrance, and

Wealth: the equipment, clothes, weapons, and other items you carry. You gain starting Trappings from your Class and Career, and can buy or find more during play (see page 297). Record each item’s Encumbrance and make sure you can carry it all (see page 299). Wealth is measured in brass pennies, silver shillings, and gold crowns.

Spells and Prayers: magical or religious Careers give access to Spells (see page 240) or Prayers (see page 220).

Talents: special abilities, tricks and techniques with individual game impacts (see page 114).

Ambition: your Character’s goals and dreams (see page 41). Party Ambition is what keeps your party together — the goal or agenda you share in common.

Wounds: how much damage you can take before suffering Critical Injuries. Your starting maximum Wounds are calculated from your Strength Bonus, Toughness Bonus (doubled), Willpower Bonus, and any other modifiers, such as the Hardy Talent (see page 40).

Damage reduces your Wounds, while Healing restores them, up to your maximum (see page 170). Increasing your Characteristics or gaining certain Talents can increase your maximum Wounds. If you take Damage when you have 0 Wounds, you suffer a Critical Injury (see page 171). Record any Critical Injuries and their effects in the large box.

Armour: Write the total Armour Points (APs) in each location on the diagram. Armour Points reduce the damage you take from weapons.

name: Choosing Class and Career
text:
Your Character’s Career is how they earn a living and fit into the world. Each Career belongs to a Class — a grouping of related occupations and ways of life. It’s easier to move between Careers within a Class, and your starting Class gives you some of your belongings.

A) Choose a Class and Career available to your Species or B) Roll on your Species’ Class and Career Table.

C) If you keep the first result, you may start the game with two Trappings (page 39) from that Career’s second Career Level.

D) If not, roll twice more and choose any of the three options to acquire one Trapping from the second Career Level instead. If you reject those as well, keep rolling until you accept a result, or simply choose one, but you gain no additional Trappings. Don’t worry, you’ll acquire enough gear to get started later.

If you acquired a Trapping in this way, tick a box (or two!) on the Career Advancement Tracker. This is the only time you may do so during Character Creation.

name: Career Level
text:
Every Career contains four levels — you begin at the first, and can advance through the other levels by spending XP (page 191) and acquiring Trappings. This increases your Status, and grants access to new Talents and Skills, as well as additional Characteristics to improve.

Copy the following to your Character Sheet in the appropriate place:

Your Class and Career, and note your Career’s page in the rulebook as you will refer back to it Note which 3 Characteristics you can advance in the first level of your Career — these are the most important to your starting Career Skills Tick the boxes on your Character Sheet next to the 10 Skills listed in the first level of your Career — these are your Career Skills. If the Skills aren’t printed on your sheet, it means they are Advanced or Group Skills, which you must write onto the sheet in the box provided Your Career’s Status (Brass/Silver/Gold) and Standing (the number after Status)

name: Generating Characteristics
text:
A) Roll 2d10 for each of the ten Characteristics in order and make a note of the results. If you are happy with these results, add each value to the appropriate Species modifier from the Characteristic Table, and record the totals on your Character Sheet.

If you stop here, note the three marked Characteristics from your first Career Level. Increase the starting level of these Characteristics by up to six in total — so increasing one by six, all three by two each, or any combination you wish.

If you’re not content and want to swap some numbers around, go to step B. If you want to roll again, go to step C.

B) Rearrange the results from step A and assign them to Characteristics of your choice, then add the appropriate Species modifiers and record the totals on your Character Sheet. You may then increase the three Characteristics from your first Career Level by up to three in total, as above.

C) Roll ten new Characteristic scores and assign them as in step B, or ignore the dice and distribute 100 points between the ten Characteristics (minimum 4, maximum 16 in each). Add the appropriate Species modifiers and record the totals on your Character Sheet. You gain no other increases to your Characteristics during character creation.

name: Starting Skill Advances
text:
Your Skills are used frequently in the game to determine if you succeed when you are trying to do something. Rolling equal to or under the target number based on your Skill gives success, so the higher your Skill number the better.

A Skill’s starting value is equal to its associated Characteristic. Each Advance increases a Skill by +5.

Your starting Skill Advances come from your Species and Career: Assign the Advances listed for your Species (pages 26–35). Assign 8 Advances among the Career Skills you selected in step 2 (page 36).

You may assign more than one Advance to the same Skill, but no Skill can receive more than 3 Advances (+15) during Character Creation.

When you have allocated all your Advances, complete the Skills section of your Character Sheet. Record the value of each associated Characteristic, including any Characteristic Advances (you’ll buy these with XP during play), then add any Skill Advances to determine the Skill’s total value.

Example: Athletics is based on Agility (Ag). If your Ag is 37 after any Characteristic Advances, and you assign 2 Advances (+10) to Athletics, your final Athletics Skill is 47.

name: Characteristic Bonuses
text:
The first or ‘tens’ digit of each Characteristic is its bonus value. Characteristic Bonuses are used in a variety of different ways throughout the rules.

Example: Strength (S) 39 equates to a Strength Bonus of 3. Willpower (WP) of 51 equals a Willpower Bonus of 5.

name: Comparing Characteristics
text: A Characteristic score of 30 is the Human average, with a score of 40 indicating a gifted individual, and a sore of 60 or more being truly exceptional. Non-human Species have different ranges of ability — the average Elf is far more graceful than the most humans, and Dwarfs are far more strong willed.

name: Starting Talents and Trappings
text:
Talents are your special abilities, tricks, and techniques with individual game impacts (see page 114). Choose a Talent from the first level of your Career and add it to your Character Sheet.

Trappings are your equipment, clothes, weapons, and other carried items.

All Characters begin with Clothing, a Dagger, and a Pouch. You also begin play with all of the Trappings from your Career’s first level. Finally, you start with some Trappings common to your Class, as shown in the Class Trappings table.

You begin the game with an amount of coins decided by your Status:

Money can be used to purchase more Trappings or saved for spending during play. Commonly available items and the relative worth of different coins are covered in Chapter 11: Consumer Guide.

name: Types Of Skills
text:
If the Skills aren’t printed on your sheet, it means they are Advanced or Group Skills, which you must write onto the sheet in the box provided.

Basic Skills can be used by any Character, even without Advances in the Skill

Advanced Skills can only be used by Characters with an Advance in the Skill

Group Skills cover broad areas, and you choose a specialization when you gain Advances, for example Lore (Empire) or Lore (Tilea)

name: Creating A Magician Or Priest
text:
If you are creating a Character who is a spellcaster or miracle worker of some sort, bear in mind that you will need to meet a short list of minimum requirements in order to work your magic from the start of your adventuring career.

A spellcaster has various options in order to cast a Spell, such as reading from grimoires, but a sensible starting suite of abilities would include:

The Second Sight Talent, without which you may not perceive the Winds of Magic.

At least one advance in the Language (Magick) Skill.

At least one advance in the Channelling Skill, with a specialisation appropriate to the type of magic you wish to work with. For example, a Wizard using the Lore of Shadows would need Channelling (Ulgu).

The Petty Magic Talent, in order to begin learning spells to cast.

This may be quite a lot to acquire as a starting character, but once you have the necessary Skills and Talents you will be able to increase your repertoire of spells when you gain experience. See Chapter 8: Magic for details of the effects of Spells and how to cast them.

Priests have a slightly easier time, reflecting the fact that their Blessings and Miracles are not as varied and powerful as Spells. In order to begin play as a Priest capable of working Blessings a Character will need:

The Bless (Deity) Talent, appropriate to the god you have chosen to worship.

At least one advance in the Pray Skill.

See Chapter 7: Religion and Belief for details of Blessings, and how to work Miracles.

name: Starting carrying capacity
text:
This measures how much you can comfortably carry without being slowed down and tired out.

Maximum Encumbrance = Strength Bonus (SB) + Toughness Bonus (TB)

Dwarfs, and Characters with the Sturdy Talent, double this figure.

You must account for the Encumbrance of any items you routinely carry around with you, reducing the Encumbrance value of any worn items by 1. The rules for Encumbrance, and the effects of being over-encumbered, are listed on page 299.

name: Starting Movement
text:
Movement is used to determine your Walk and Run speed. If using a grid for movement, this indicates how many squares you can move in a Round. If not using a grid, it indicates how many inches across the tabletop. When you Run, you double these distances.

Example: A human with a Movement of 4 can walk 4 squares or run 8 squares per Round on a grid. If not using a grid, they can walk 4 inches or run 8 inches per Round.

Over the longer term it indicates how many miles per hour you can comfortably travel on foot. For more on Movement, see page 156, and 162 for moving in comabt.

name: Oh Fickle Fate
text: Some say that gods reward those who allow their hand to shape lives and guide actions. If you chose to accept the first random result for each of your Species, Career, and Characteristics, increase your Fate by 1.

name: Starting Wounds
text:
Wounds show how much Damage you can take before you suffer serious injury.

Wounds = Strength Bonus (SB) + Willpower Bonus (WPB) + 2 × Toughness Bonus (TB)

So, if you have 34 Strength, 27 Willpower and 38 Toughness, your Wounds would be 3+2+3+3=11. If you have the Hardy Talent, add your Toughness Bonus again.

Write your Wounds total on your Character Sheet.

name: Achieving Your Ambitions
text:
At the end of any session in which you make genuine progress towards your ambition, the GM should reward you with an additional 50 XP. This should be real, measurable, and substantial progress. Killing one of the five mercenaries who slew your parents is real progress towards a vengeful Ambition. Buying a sword with the intent of going after them is not.

Achieving your Ambition rewards you with an additional 250 XP. This is a moment to decide if your Character’s story has reached its end, and if you’d prefer to retire them and continue your campaign with a new Character. If not, choose a new Ambition that gets your Character back out into the world and facing down its dangers.

name: Choose an Ambition
text:
An Ambition is your Character’s goal in life — what they want to achieve. It helps define what is important to your Character, and making progress towards or achieving your Ambition earns additional XP.

Choose a long-term goal your Character may work towards for months or even years, and may even never achieve. Discuss your Ambition with your GM to make sure it is significant enough and fits your game. If inspiration strikes, you can change your Ambition between sessions.

Examples include: Owning your own coaching inn. Building your village into a thriving town. Ridding the Colleges of Magic of Elven influence.

name: Party Ambition
text:
A Party Ambition is a long-term goal shared by the whole group, which binds you together. It might be based on shared beliefs or a common enemy, or be as practical as earning a living.

Discuss your Party Ambition with the GM as a group, to make sure it fits the campaign. Unlike a personal Ambition, making progress towards a Party Ambition grants no XP. Completing it, however, gives the incredibly rare reward of an additional Fate Point for each Character.

name: Tests
text: At the core of the rules are Tests. Can you persuade a suspicious watchman to let you pass, or decipher the arcane inscriptions on a book that murmurs in the voice of the witch who wrote it? Routine actions and anything with an obvious outcome simply succeed, without the need for a Test. When the outcome of an action is uncertain or opposed by another character, you make a Test.

name: Describe Action
text: • Player describes what their Character is trying to do. • GM determines if a Test is required. If it is, GM explains any factors affecting the action that would be obvious to the Character. • If the player still wishes to proceed, the GM decides what Skill or Characteristic to Test.

name: Roll Dice
text: • Player rolls the dice, a d100, trying to get equal or lower than their Skill. If they do, they have succeeded. • If it’s important to know how well or badly they did, we use the Test’s Success Level (SL). Subtract the first digit of your roll from the first digit of the Skill or Characteristic being tested to see how many SL you’ve generated, as shown below.

name: Difficulty And Character Modifiers
text: Not all Tests are as simple as the one above. The Success Level of a Test can be modified by how difficult it is to succeed, or by the Character’s abilities and equipment: • Difficulty — set by the GM, with easier tasks giving an SL bonus and harder ones giving a penalty (see Difficulty Table). • Character’s modifiers — come from Talents, equipment, Spells, and other effects. These will be clear on the player’s Character Sheet. Combine any SL bonuses or penalties from the Difficulty with the Character’s modifiers to arrive at the final SL modifier for the roll. This could turn a success into a failure, or prise victory from the jaws of defeat!

name: Summary & Outcome
text: • Rolling equal to or under your Skill gives you positive SL, rolling above it gives you negative SL. • Difficulty or Character modifiers adjust the SL • A positive SL result means you succeed, and a negative SL result means you fail. Often, you will only need to know whether a Test results in a success or failure. If it’s important to know just how well you have passed, or how badly you have failed, consult the Outcomes Table below. The GM uses the descriptions in the table to decide what happens as a result of your action. There are lots of example outcome tables for a variety of actions, along with specific advice on how to use the rules, later in this chapter.

name: Rolling with Advantage
text:
Molli ducks into an alley to hide from some approaching guards. Her Alley Cat Talent lets her make Stealth (Urban) Test with

Advantage. Molli’s Stealth (Urban) Skill is 46 and she rolls a 72. Normally this would be a failure, but Advantage allows her to reverse the numbers for a result of 27 — a success!

Disadvantage works the same way, but you must reverse the results if they would be worse. So if Molli suffered from Disadvantage on a Test, then a roll of 18 would be reversed to result in an 81 instead.

name: Typical Test
text: Martha is playing Markus Kurtentaager, a Reiklander merchant attempting to make her way through Altdorf without attracting the attention of anyone she owes money to. She tells the GM that Markus is sticking to quiet streets, wearing a hood, and otherwise trying not to be seen — the GM rules that’s an Average (+2 SL) Stealth (Urban) Test. Markus has Stealth (Urban) 39, and rolls a 41. That’s -1 SL, as the result on the dice is higher, and 3 - 4 = -1. That’s normally a failure, but adding +2 SL because the Test is of Average Difficulty makes it a success (+1 SL). The GM tells Martha that no one seems to have realised Markus is in town… yet.

name: Spend a Fortune Point to:
text: Gain Advantage on a Test before rolling. Reroll a Test, keeping the new result. You may spend another Fortune to reroll again. Remove one Condition (page 184).

name: Using The Rules
text:
The core rules on the preceding pages are everything you need to know to start playing Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay. The following sections cover specific applications of the rules in greater detail, and deal with the situations you are most likely to encounter.

Theft and Skullduggery, page 134 Flattery, Bribery, and Status, page 140 Nosing Around, page 146 Life Beyond the Walls, page 152 Cunning Crafts, page 153 Getting Around, page 156 Combat, page 161 Injury, Healing, and Death, page 170 Disease and Infection, page 179 Psychology, page 183 Conditions, page 184 Corruption and Mutation, page 187

name: A Time For Crime
text:
If a Character earns their living through crime, such as a Thief or Charlatan, treat it like any other Career. Their routine work is resolved during Downtime using the Income Endeavour.

There is no need to roleplay picking the pocket of every NPC they encounter — that would quickly become frustrating for the other players!

name: Common Forms Of Skullduggery
text:
| Action | Test |
| --- | --- |
| Pick a pocket | A Sleight of Hand Test, opposed by your target’s Perception. |
| Force open a door or window | A Strength Test to do it quickly, or a Stealth (Urban) Test with the right tools to do it quietly. |
| Pick a lock | A Pick Lock Test, with a difficulty set by the lock’s quality. Especially challenging locks might require an Extended Test, with one roll every round, or every minute. |
| Connect with local criminals | A Difficult (-1 SL) Gossip Test, made with Advantage if you have the Criminal Talent yourself. |
| Argue your innocence | A Charm Test, opposed by your opponent’s Cool, or an opposed Lore (Law) Test to do so in court. Either way, Test with Disadvantage if you were caught red-handed or if there is incriminating evidence. |
| Cheat at cards | A Sleight of Hand Test, opposed by your opponent’s Perception. Success grants Advantage on your next Gamble Test during that game. |
| Bribe a guard | A Bribery Test to find someone open to being bribed, at a price set by their status. You might Haggle with them over the price. |
| Learn a thing’s value | An Evaluate Test to learn something’s value, or a Difficult (-1 SL) Evaluate Test to quickly spot the most valuable thing in a room. |

name: Theft And Skullduggery
text:
Crime is common in the Empire. Some say anything not nailed down is likely to be stolen, but that overlooks the thriving second-hand market for questionably acquired nails.

Characters are likely to break the law from time to time, often for good reason. A crime may even be the focus of an adventure, such as breaking into a wealthy merchant’s home to uncover evidence of cult activity. In such cases, every detail matters, from breaking in and searching for hidden evidence to escaping unseen.

There is often no need to make a Test when time is not an issue or failure has few consequences. For example, if the players steal a locked chest, you can simply say they force it open once they have time, rather than requiring a Pick Lock Test.

name: Example Difficulties Of Common Underhanded Tasks
text:
| Difficulty | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Very Easy (+6 SL) | Sleight of Hand: Steal bread from a helpless urchin. Charm: Convince an already furious mob to set fire to something. Bribe: Find a corrupt tax inspector on the docks in Übersreik. |
| Easy (+4 SL) | Stealth (Urban): Vanish into a crowded street at night. Lore (Law): Explain you can’t be arrested solely for looking suspicious. Intimidate: Threaten a common thief into bothering someone less well-armed. |
| Average (+2 SL) | Sleight of Hand: Run a common scam, like cups or Manaan’s Shells. Perception: Spot an ogre moving through a nearby street. Gossip: Find the name of a wealthy merchant or other tempting mark. |

name: Worked example — Stealth (Rural)
text: A Stealth (Rural) Test to infiltrate a guarded manor house. Astounding Success (+5 SL): You sneak inside and happen upon a servant’s livery drying on the line — the perfect disguise should you wish to explore the living quarters. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): You sneak inside and notice a poorly guarded garden path you can later use to make a quick escape. Success (+1 to +2 SL): You sneak inside the manor without being seen. Marginal Success (+0 SL): You sneak inside, but leave signs of your entrance that will surely be noticed come morning. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): You fail to find a safe way inside, but manage to avoid being spotted by the guards during your attempt. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): You’re discovered by a guard who spots you from across the courtyard. Time to run! Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): You stumble into the path of a patrol, who bellow a warning to the estate before drawing the blades and bearing down on you. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): A misplaced step sees you tumbling from a watch house roof and right into the path of the captain of the guards, who recognises you on the spot.

name: Worked example — Sleight of Hand
text: A Sleight of Hand Test to cheat at cards. Astounding Success (+5 SL): You grant yourself enough cards to win any game you wish without making a Gamble Test at all. You could even frame another character for cheating, if you like! Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): You pocket enough high cards to grant yourself Advantage on any Gamble Tests you make during the night’s merriment. Success (+1 to +2 SL): You pocket a pair of useful cards, granting you Advantage on your next Gamble Test. Marginal Success (+0 SL): You gain Advantage on your next Gamble Test, but one of your opponents grows suspicious of you. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): You pass off a failed palming of a card as mere clumsiness. Your opponents are all suspicious of you and watch you carefully from now on. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): You are caught cheating by at least two of your opponents, who immediately call for your winnings to be confiscated, and you are kicked out into the frigid night. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): Your cheating is obvious for all to see, and your opponents offer you two ways out — a night in the stocks, or a duel on the morrow. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): A mistimed flourish sees pocketed cards spill from your coat for all to see. The bar erupts in an uproar, and a fight breaks out over who gets to gut you first.

If no difficulty is specified, or if the trap was left long ago or by an unknown person, the Difficulty is Challenging (+0 SL). Exceedingly obvious traps, or those set in extremely barren areas or open plains with few places to hide the mechanisms involved, may only require an Average (+2 SL) or easier Perception Test.

name: Worked example — Secret Signs
text: A Secret Signs Test to gather information on local thieves Astounding Success (+5 SL): As below, and you find subtle signs designed to misdirect most, but which point to another thief’s cache. It contains a pouch of 1d10 Silver Shillings nestled between a crowbar and a length of rope. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): As below, and you also discover which streets are the most carefully patrolled by the town watch. Success (+1 to +2 SL): You spot some signs pointing to a local bar frequented by the criminal underworld, where you can doubtless learn more. Marginal Success (+0 SL): You spot signs indicating the way to a local bar, but draw undue attention from someone else — a wary burgher, or perhaps a fellow thief. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): You fail to spot any hidden signs, but a local vagabond notices what you’re doing. Laughing, he points you in the right direction, but spreads word that you’re somewhat of a fool. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): You spot nothing, but avoid drawing undue attention to yourself. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): You misread a sign and end up in a bar frequented by the town watch. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): You completely misread some signs and find yourself stumbling into the den of the most notorious and least welcoming gang boss in town.

name: Criminal Coinage
text:
Counterfeit currency is common, often involving coating a base metal, such as lead, in a thin layer of gold or silver. Real currency is sometimes debased by clipping, removing a small amount of precious metal from the edges. Merchants are on the lookout for such things, and a successful Evaluate Test reveals if a payment contains any obviously dodgy currency.

When forging coinage, a Hard (-2 SL) Art (Engraving) Test is made to create a convincing die, followed by a Trade (Smith) Test to strike the coins. Unless relevant to the events of an adventure, this is best handled via the Income Endeavour (page 199).

name: Worked example — Charm
text: A Charm Test to convince a merchant to invest their coin with you Astounding Success (+5 SL): The merchant invests ten gold crowns in your scheme and convinces an even more credulous business partner to invest ten more. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): The merchant is so impressed by your scheme that he immediately places ten gold crowns with you. Success (+1 to +2 SL): The merchant happily parts with the five gold crowns you sought. Marginal Success (+0 SL): You convince your mark to invest a gold crown, but he’d like to invite his brother into the opportunity as well, who just so happens to be an officer in the town watch. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): You fail to secure the coin, but the merchant isn’t aware you were trying to con him. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): The merchant passes on your investment and advises colleagues to avoid you. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): The merchant sees right through your scam and reports you to the town watch. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): The merchant avoids your obvious scam, but recognises your enthusiasm, if not your talent. He offers you a deal — help him con his partner, or he will report you to the city watch himself.

text:
| Action | Test |
| --- | --- |
| Befriend a useful contact | A Charm Test to make a good impression, discover what someone likes, or otherwise ingratiate yourself with them. This could yield useful information or grant Advantage on a future Test. |
| Make someone Fear you | An Intimidate Test, opposed by the target’s Cool. |
| Carouse with some soldiers | A Perform, Play or Entertain Test to regale them with songs, music, or stories, or a Consume Alcohol Test to join the festivities and prove you can keep up. |
| Convince someone to do what you want | A Charm Test to convince them to see things your way, opposed by the subject’s Cool. A suitable Lore Test may replace Charm when it comes to intellectual debates, while Intimidate may get you what you want in the short term, but leave you with a longer term problem. |
| Talk your way in to a gathering | A Charm Test, opposed by your opponent’s Cool. The Difficulty depends on whether you look as though you belong, and how plausible your reasoning is for getting inside. |
| Inspire a crowd | A Charm Test, opposed by the lowest Cool rating of those listening. Leadership can be used in a military setting or when you otherwise have authority over the gathered crowd. |
| Read the Room | An Intuition Test to determine the general mood of a group of people, figure out who holds power, who is happy to follow their lead, and who’s afraid of whom. |

| Spread a Nasty Rumour | A Gossip Test, with a difficulty depending on how hard the rumour is to believe and what evidence you might have to support it. |
| Negotiate a Discount | A Haggle Test to convince the merchant to offer you a better rate. |

name: Difficulty Factors of Social Tests
text:
Use the following table as a guide when setting the Difficulty of a Social Test. Positive factors make a Test easier, while negative factors make it harder. These are only guidelines. The GM has the final say, and some NPCs will simply never agree to a Character’s demands, no matter how charming or intimidating they may be.

Add up the positive factors, and subtract the negative. If you are left with a positive number, the Test should be Average (+2 SL) or Easy (+4 SL). If you are left with a negative number, the Test should be Difficult (-1 SL), Hard (-2 SL), or Very Hard (-3 SL).

name: Flattery, Bribery, And Status
text:
Conversations between Characters and NPCs are at the heart of WFRP. If a Character says the right thing, or asks for something an NPC has no reason to refuse, there is usually no need for a Test. Asking a bystander about recent events or a merchant the price of their wares, for example, simply works.

A Test is only needed when the request involves risk, effort, or persuasion, or when gathering valuable or dangerous information (see Asking Around, page 150).

| Difficult (-1 SL) | Leadership: Order your soldiers to hold in the face of an oncoming cavalry charge. Charm: Convince an enemy soldier to hear you out before they gut you. Consume Alcohol: Match a dwarf, drink for drink. |

name: Worked example — Charm
text: A Charm Test to make a good impression at a courtly ball. Astounding Success (+5 SL): You are the life of the party, your wit and good graces a highlight of the evening for many. You depart having been introduced to many noteworthy individuals, and with an invitation to at least one private dinner. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): You seamlessly fit in with those present, joining conversations as though you were an old friend. Many wonder why they haven’t seen you at such events before. Success (+1 to +2 SL): You fit in well, receiving a few mostly sincere invitations to future events, and inviting polite inquiries into your own interests and agenda. Marginal Success (+0 SL): You acquit yourself well, recalling an anecdote that saw a polite chuckle cross the room. Most view you as at least somewhat interesting. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): You fade into the general patter of the court, unable to make yourself seen, but at least learning the names of some important individuals you might pursue directly. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): Your clumsy attempts at inserting yourself into the court’s good graces fall flat. Most barely remember you were there at all. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): You embarrass yourself terribly, spilling wine on both yourself and a lady of the court. You come off as something of a fool, unworthy of time or attention. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): A careless word or scathing insult leaves many present aghast at your indiscretion. You earn a foul reputation with at least one NPC or faction present.

name: Worked example — Intimidate
text: An Intimidate Test to convince a merchant to close up shop Astounding Success (+5 SL): The merchant is terrified of you, and departs the town that very night, perhaps leaving behind several valuables in their haste to get away from you. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): The merchant, certain their life is on the line, asks for a few days to get their affairs in order, but otherwise agrees to your demands. Success (+1 to +2 SL): The merchant agrees, at least for now, and closes their premises. Marginal Success (+0 SL): The merchant takes your threats seriously, but attempts to extort you for a substantial sum of money before they will consider closing their store. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): The merchant does not think your threats are credible, but offers you a pittance of a bribe to simply be on your way. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): The merchant assumes you are simply trying to shake them down, and offers a small bribe, while intenting to spell a larger sum on hiring some protection. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): The merchant laughs, draws a weapon, and orders you out into the street while calling loudly for the guards. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): Your half-hearted threats are seen as rank weakness, and the merchant laughs in your face, or offers to duel you right now and settle the matter outright.

name: Worked example — Charm
text: A Charm Test to convince a noble to support your claim to a mine Astounding Success (+5 SL): The noble is entirely taken in by your talk of injustice, and sees enough benefit to their reputation should they aid your cause that they seek nothing in return. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): The noble is impressed by your daring in attempting to enlist their aid, and supports your claim, though they make it clear you owe them a favour. Success (+1 to +2 SL): The noble agrees to support your claim, so long as they receive a stipend from the mine once its operation is returned to you. Marginal Success (+0 SL): The noble agrees that your claim seems just and legal, but pointedly wonders aloud what could possibly be in it for them… Marginal Failure (-0 SL): The noble finds your petition tedious and casually mentions that they are far too preoccupied with a rival’s machinations to bother with yours. Of course, if you could somehow help them with that matter, they might reconsider… Failure (-1 to -2 SL): The noble has no interest in your foolish errand and refuses to lend you any aid. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): The noble is offended by your pathetic attempts at intrigue and actively opposes your claim when the matter next arises at court. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): The noble is insulted you’d try to draw them into your petty squabble, and vows to claim the mine for themselves.

name: Success And Consequence
text: Charm, Intimidate, and similar Skills are not mind control. A successful Test can make someone more helpful, compliant, or fearful, but most people will not risk everything for a stranger. Success also has consequences. A convincing lie falls apart when the truth comes to light, and those bullied or intimidated into helping you may later seek revenge — or simply inform the authorities.

name: Worked example — Hard (-2 SL) Gossip
text:
A Hard (-2 SL) Gossip Test to spread word that an unpleasant but quite mundane merchant is actually a vampire Astounding Success (+5 SL): The merchant is dragged off in silver chains by a witch hunter and, by the time they have proven themselves innocent, is left without a shilling to their name. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): Cruel or fearful glances follow the merchant everywhere, and their business suffers. They are jostled or even attacked in the streets, and at least consider leaving town. Success (+1 to +2 SL): Rumours abound in high and low places of the merchant’s crimes. An enterprising individual could likely rally an angry mob — see Public Speaking, page 145. Marginal Success (+0 SL): The rumour is widely spread but only rarely believed. Still, unkind words and unpleasant japes dog the merchant for months. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): Most find the idea too ridiculous to be believed, but at least one gullible soul takes up your tale and shares it with any other fool they should happen across.

Failure (-1 to -2 SL): The rumour never takes hold.

Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): The rumour is not believed, and people think less of you for trying to spread such fearmongering tales about an innocent man.

Astounding Failure (-5 SL): The rumour is not believed, and word gets back to the merchant of just who has been attempting to smear their name.

name: Worked example — Hard (-2 SL) Charm
text:
A Hard (-2 SL) Charm Test to convince a gathered crowd to support your appointment as village alderman. Astounding Success (+5 SL): You are lifted aloft by the exultant crowd and paraded through the streets, with most convinced there could be no better candidate for the position. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): Most are convinced by your words, and a few are truly passionate, telling their friends and acquaintances to support you. Success (+1 to +2 SL): You make a good impression, leaving most convinced you’d make a decent alderman. Marginal Success (+0 SL): People come away generally favourable towards your bid for the position, but could be easily swayed towards someone more compelling.

Marginal Failure (-0 SL): A few people seem to nod on occasion, but no one leaves convinced you’d be suitable.

Failure (-1 to -2 SL): You fail to convince almost anyone that you would be a suitable alderman. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): Most people leave convinced that almost anyone other than you would be preferable. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): Rotten fruit, clumps of dirt, and anything else people can lay their hands on are tossed your way as you completely botch your attempt to curry favour.

name: Stinking Drunk
text:
| 1d10 | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| 1–2 | ‘Marienburger’s Courage!’: Gain a bonus of +2 SL to resist Fear. |
| 3–4 | ‘You’re My Besht Mate!’: Ignore all your existing Animosities (see page 183). |
| 5–6 | ‘Why’s Everything Wobbling!’: On your Turn, you can either Move or take an Action, but not both (see page 162). |
| 7–8 | ‘I’ll Take Yer All On!’: Gain Animosity (Everybody!) (see page 183). |
| 9–10 | ‘How Did I Get Here?’: You wake up the next day, massively hungover, with little memory of what transpired. The GM and other players with you will fill in the embarrassing gaps if you investigate. Pass a Consume Alcohol Test or also gain a Poisoned Condition (see page 186). |

name: Common Means Of Investigation And Research
text:
| Action | Test |
| --- | --- |
| Tell how an animal died | An Average (+2 SL) Animal Care Test, or Challenging (+0 SL) if a subtle poison or illness was the cause. |
| Tell a lie, or spot one | The liar makes a Charm Test, opposed by the target’s Intuition. The Difficulty can increase if the lie is particularly outrageous. |
| Ask around about someone | A Gossip Test to learn what others think of the subject, with better rolls revealing more secretive or pertinent information. A successful Bribery Test can tell you someone is corrupt enough to take a bribe, and what their price might be. |
| Wring a secret from someone | A Charm Test, opposed by the target’s Cool to trick them into letting something slip, or an Intimidate Test opposed by Cool to force the information from them. The Difficulty is set by just how sensitive the information is. |
| Search a room or a crime scene | A successful Perception Test spots hidden or subtle details, with better results revealing more information. A disturbed scene increases the Test’s Difficulty. |
| Extract information from books | A successful Research Test will tell you what library or book to consult to learn something, or help you find pertinent facts buried within large and mouldering tomes. |
| Recall a useful fact | Having an Advance in a Lore Skill will tell you basic information about that subject, with a Test required only to recall particularly obscure or unusual information. |
| Spot a forgery | An Evaluate Test, with a Difficulty set by the quality of the work. |
| Follow someone’s trail | A Track Test, with a Difficulty set by the conditions and age of the trail. Opposed by your quarry’s Track only if they took the time to cover their trail. |

name: Hiding Clues
text:
Don’t hide vital clues behind a Test. It can be tempting to make Players work for information, but if finding that information is essential to the adventure, they should find it.

Instead, allow Characters to notice one or two important clues straight away. Use Perception or Intuition Tests to reveal additional clues, useful insights, or a clearer understanding of what has already been discovered.

Let the Players piece the evidence together where possible, and if they still become stuck, provide another lead. If all else fails, a helpful NPC can always point the way. An unsolved mystery is intriguing — one the Characters never discover is simply frustrating.

name: Battle Tongue
text:
Battle Tongue is a specialised language that conveys complex tactical information in just a few words. A Character who passes a Challenging (+0 SL) Language (Battle) Test can use their Action to communicate up to 40 words of orders or tactical advice to others who know Language (Battle).

If players spend too long discussing tactics during combat, the GM can remind them that only Characters with Battle Tongue can exchange detailed plans in the heat of battle.

The following are the most common languages of the Old World, and the peoples who speak them. Many other tongues exist, but these are the ones most often encountered in the Reikland.

name: Common Lore Specialisations
text:
| Specialisation | Information Provided |
| --- | --- |
| Engineering | Understand the application of levers, pulleys, inclined planes, and other simple machinery. Recognise the work of a specific artisan, or the principles underlying a complex machine. |
| Geology | Recognise specific types of stone, and determine where digging a well or mine is likely to prove fruitful, or judge if a cave is prone to flooding or likely to collapse. |
| Heraldry | Recognise the banners and iconography of great noble houses and military outfits. Determine the meaning of the animals, colours, and other symbols used in a coat of arms. |
| History | Recall pertinent facts about historical events. |
| Law | Know what the law is and how it might be broken or circumvented, and make a compelling legal argument or recognise the flaw in one. |
| Magic | Recall the names of the Winds of Magic and their effects, recognise the trappings of a particular magical tradition, or determine if a grimoire contains true spells or the ravings of the mad. |
| Metallurgy | Determine what metals or alloys a weapon or tool is made of, how it was likely to have been forged, and how it might be repaired. |
| Science | Knowledge of natural philosophy — how the mundane phenomena appear to work, and the theory behind creating unusual compounds such as black powder or soap. |
| Theology | The practices and beliefs behind religions common to your culture, such as Sigmar, Taal, or Ulric, worshipped in the Empire, or Asuryan and Khaine, who are revered by the elves. |

name: Worked example — Average (+2 SL) Gossip
text: An Average (+2 SL) Gossip Test to gather rumours about a nearby mine Astounding Success (+5 SL): All of the below, along with tales of strange folk descending into the mine each Gheimisnacht for reasons better left unlearned. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): You learn the below, plus the name of one of the former miners who still lives nearby. Success (+1 to +2 SL): You learn that the mine was closed after a series of unusual deaths that saw labourers refuse to enter it. Marginal Success (+0 SL): You learn that the mine closed a decade ago, but not why. Marginal Failure (-0 SL): You learn nothing about the mine, but do notice that people seem reticent to talk about it, as though it is ill-omened in some way. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): You learn nothing of use. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): Rumours begin to circulate that you’re a wealthy merchant interested in local mines, leading to several distracting and unhelpful inquiries from local labourers and land owners. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): You waste the night drinking with a man who claims to know everything there is to know about the mine, only to learn that he was talking about a quarry three days’ walk towards Altdorf.

name: Good Roleplay
text:
Good and entertaining roleplay should be rewarded with useful information whenever appropriate, without requiring a Test. If the information is especially valuable or dangerous, a Challenging (+0 SL) Charm Test or a suitable bribe may be needed instead.

Players who prefer to rely on their Character’s abilities rather than acting in character should still explain what they are trying to say or ask before making a Test. The GM can then decide whether a Test is required, and if so, which Skill and Difficulty are appropriate..

name: Worked example — Challenging (+0 SL) Perception
text:
A Challenging (+0 SL) Perception Test to search the scene of a murder Astounding Success (+5 SL): All of the below, and you spot flecks of unusual purple paint or dye beneath the fingernails — a rare substance available in very few places. Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL): As below, but you also notice two indents on the victim’s nose — a sign that they wore spectacles, and were likely a learned man of some kind. Success (+1 to +2 SL): As below, and you additionally notice that there is not enough blood to account for how deep the wounds are — he was almost certainly killed elsewhere, then moved here.

Marginal Success (+0 SL): You spot the body and notice that it appears to have been moved.

Marginal Failure (-0 SL): You spot the dead body and notice there is something odd in how it lies, but can’t say how. Failure (-1 to -2 SL): You notice the body, but learn nothing of use. Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL): You notice the dead body, but become convinced that some irrelevant detail, such as a discarded cup, may be important. Astounding Failure (-5 SL): You notice the dead body, but manage to leave bloody footprints throughout the room, muddying the scene and leaving evidence of your own presence in the process.

name: Life Beyond The Walls
text: Beyond the walls of the cities and towns of the Empire, the landscape is anything but welcoming. Aside from a few hardy farmers, daring merchants, and cautious Roadwardens, travellers are unlikely to meet a friendly face among the bandits and beastmen that trouble them. Occasional relief can be had at a price from Coaching Houses along the Empire’s highways, but otherwise Characters must fend for themselves.

name: Cunning Crafts
text:
Life may be cheap in the Empire, but the necessities of living are anything but. Most commoners are used to making what they can for themselves and purchasing only those essentials they can’t get by without. Clothes, simple tools, and damp hovels of mud and stone are often made by their owners, while skilled artisans create more complicated and hard wearing goods.

Smiths, artisans, and others who make their living by creating things for others can use the Income Endeavour (page 199) to reflect their typical business operations. Creating particular items, such as a sword, armour, or wagon, can be handled via the Crafting Endeavour (page 198). If there is enough time during an adventure, the GM can allow a character to undertake a Crafting Endeavour during play if they wish.

During an adventure, characters may wish to quickly create something they desperately need that they either cannot afford or find. An appropriate Trade Test, with a difficulty set by the complexity of the item being created, is usually sufficient. As most items take time and resources to create, the GM should rule on what is reasonable in a given situation. A skilled character in a well equipped workshop could reasonably create a simple blade with an Average (+2 SL) Trade (Smith) Test, while a Very Hard (-3 SL) Trade (Shipwright) Test would be required to lash together a small raft just from materials gathered at the river’s edge.

Some other common situations are covered below.

(+2 SL) Climb Test. You will Climb an extra Movement + SL yards. So, a character with Movement 4 who rolled +2 SL will climb an additional 6 yards (4+2=6).

If both hands are free, you can climb other surfaces with suitable handholds with a Climb Test using your Action for the Turn. You ascend or descend at a rate of ½ Movement + SL in yards.

Climbing difficulty is set by the GM and varies with the nature of the climbed surface. Some climbs will be beyond the ability of most characters without the Scale Sheer Surface Talent (see page 125).

name: Getting Around
text:
You have to keep on your toes to stay ahead in the Empire, whether slipping between throngs of people baying for blood at a public execution or leaping across the crumbling rooftops of Altdorf. This section deals with moving through the space immediately around you — if you want to cover longer distances, look to Navigation on page 152 instead.

No Test is required for most kinds of movement. If you want something on the other side of a room, you can simply go get it. Equally, so long as you have at least one Advance in an appropriate Ride or Drive skill, handling a mount or vehicle under normal conditions does not require the use of any dice.

Moving during combat, along with exactly how much distance you can cover in a Turn, and how to keep track of where you are on a map or with miniatures, is covered in more detail on page 163.

name: How Far, Though?
text: Generally speaking, you will only need to know if your Character made a particular jump or not. With a decent run-up and a successful Athletics Test, most Characters can leap around their Movement Characteristic in yards. Additional SL after the first can increase this by up to twice that distance, but very few save the most athletic individuals can manage further than that.

name: Rounds Outside Combat
text: Outside combat, actions do not usually need to be resolved in Rounds. The GM may use them whenever timing matters or to ensure everyone has a chance to act, however, such as during an Extended Test (page 131).

name: Attacking
text: To make a Ranged Attack, your target must be within your weapon’s range (see Chapter 11: Consumer Guide) and in your line of sight. To make a Melee Attack, you must be Engaged with your target (page 163) and have a weapon ready.

name: Damaging Weapons And Armour
text:
Damaged Weapons Some Fumble results (see page 165) or Spells may damage your weapon. For each point of Damage your weapon receives, reduce its Damage by –1. If the Damage is reduced to +0 (or +SB + 0), the weapon is mangled beyond all recognition, and now counts as an Improvised Weapon. If an Improvised Weapon is damaged, it is considered useless for melee combat.

Damaged Armour As blows rain down on your armour, it can be damaged, possibly permanently. Whenever you are instructed to damage a piece of armour, reduce the AP in the damaged Hit Location by 1.

If this lowers the AP to 0 in that Location, the armour there is rendered useless.

name: Injury, Healing, And Death
text: Getting hurt is all but unavoidable. Combat, accidents, spells gone awry, and simple bad luck can all lead to lost Wounds, hideous infections, or an untimely trip to the Garden of Morr.

name: The Heal Skill And Bleeding Conditions
text: Characters remove one Bleeding Condition for each Wound they recover. While the Heal Skill can only be used to recover Wounds once per incident, you can still use it to remove Bleeding Conditions — simply remove one for each Wound that would have been recovered.

name: Healing Animals
text: When attempting to heal an animal, follow the rules for healing as laid out here but replace the Heal Skill with the Animal Care Skill.

name: Open Wounds
text: If you lose Wounds and do not apply a Bandage (page 316) or have your injury seen to in some other way, such as by a successful use of the Heal Skill, you risk infection. At the end of the day, make an Average (+ 2 SL) Endurance Test. If you fail, you incur the Infection Symptom (page 182) until you are treated with a successful Difficult (-1 SL) Heal Test, or obtain a herbal Remedy (page 314) or other suitable cure.

name: Pulling Your Blows
text:
The rules assume you wish to inflict every possible Critical Wound you can. It is also possible you may just want to subdue, not kill, your opponents — or you may be sparring. With that in mind, you may ignore any Critical Wound you should inflict upon your opponents if you declare you are ‘pulling your blow’ before you roll to hit. If you do this, make sure you describe the situation appropriately, making it clear you are using the flat of your blade or otherwise doing what you can to avoid properly hurting your opponent.

You may not pull blows with missiles, Spells, Miracles, or weapons that cause Ablaze Conditions. The following Weapon Qualities are lost when pulling your blows: Damaging, Hack, Impact, Impale, and Penetrating.

If you are trying to knock your opponent out you will need to: 1. Declare your intention and that you are pulling your blows.

2. Hit them on the Head Location.

3. Use a weapon with the Pummel Quality.

4. Inflict more Stunned Conditions than your target’s Toughness Bonus. Or use the Silent Takedown rules (page 135).

Additional Wound Loss from Critical Wounds Use the Wounds column on the Critical Wounds table to determine additional Wounds lost as a result of that Critical Wound. Work out this extra damage after calculating all other effects of normal damage and Critical Wounds. Wounds caused in this way do not cause further rolls on the Critical Wounds table.

name: Characteristic Loss
text: Sometimes, terrible injuries, horrific spells, or other events may cause your Character to suffer a loss to their Characteristics. When this occurs, reduce the base Characteristic first. If your Character finds themselves in the unfortunate position of having a base Characteristic reduced to 0, then remove any Advances you may have purchased.

name: Healing Times And Downtime
text:
The recovery times from various Injuries are given in days and assume that you are keeping track of the number of days that have passed. Each Downtime (page 190) is about a week long, or 8 days by the Imperial calendar (page 289).

Minor You have fractured one of your bones, but it is still aligned, meaning it may heal of its own accord without Medical Attention. The Hit Location cannot be used until the breakage heals. For arm and leg hits, you are down to one limb as the other is too painful to use, and may require binding. Use the rules for an amputated arm or leg to represent this (see Amputated Parts, page 177).

For head hits, you will be down to a liquid diet and will suffer a penalty of -3 SL to all Language Tests. For body hits, your strength and mobility will be severely limited: you suffer Disadvantage on Tests based on Strength and Agility, and halve your Movement.

Healing: A fractured bone will take 30 + 1d10 days to heal. At the end of this, a successful Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test means the bone has set well, and no long-term effects will be suffered. If the Test is failed, you suffer -1 SL to all Agility Tests when using a damaged arm, a permanent loss of -1 Movement and -10 to your Agility Characteristic for a badly healed body or leg hit, or -1 SL to spoken Language Tests for a badly healed head hit.

A successful Average (+2 SL) Heal Test within a week of receiving the fracture will negate the need for the Endurance Test, but the affected area must remain bound and held in place for the duration of the healing. If the binding should be undone, another Average (+2 SL) Heal Test enacted within a day will need to be passed to avoid the Endurance Test.

Major One of your bones is badly broken, and is either resting at an odd angle, or has splintered at the point of breakage. It is unlikely to heal properly without Medical Attention. The Hit Location is effectively unusable until the breakage heals. Use all the same rules as for Broken Bone (Minor).

Healing: Healing takes 10 days longer. All associated Tests are Challenging (+0 SL). If the Test is failed, you suffer –2 SL to all Agility Tests when using a damaged arm, a permanent loss of -2 Movement and -20 to your Agility Characteristic for a badly healed body or leg hit, or -2 SL to spoken Language Tests for a badly healed head hit.

name: Impressive Scars
text: Scars and amputations are common in the Empire, and even sought out as a mark of an accomplished duelist or street tough. Should you accumulate a sufficient number of visible scars, severed appendages, and other marks of hard-lived life, and the GM agrees, you gain a permanent bonus of +1 SL to Intimidate Tests, and incur -1 SL penalty to Charm Tests.

name: Conditions And Fortune
text: A Condition can be removed with a Fortune Point, so while they are debilitating, they can be managed if you are careful (see page 133).

name: Multiple Conditions
text:
You can be subject to the same Condition more than once; indeed, sometimes you will receive multiples of the same Condition from a single event. If this occurs, any penalties suffered are stacked. So, if you have 3 Bleeding Conditions, you are losing a worrying 3 Wounds per Round; or if you have 3 Fatigued Conditions, you suffer -3 SL to all Tests.

You can also be subject to multiple, different Conditions at once. When this occurs, the effects do not stack; you suffer the highest of the two penalties and apply it. So, if you had 1 Fatigued and the Prone Condition, you would suffer a -2 SL penalty to all active Tests, not -3 SL.
