name: During Downtime
text:
Characters recover all Wounds.

Players may spend XP to purchase Characteristics, Skills, and Talents.

The GM rolls a Regional Event table to determine what’s taking place in the world around the Characters.

Each player rolls a Character Event to find out what’s happening to their Character during Downtime.

Characters may purchase items and Trappings from shops before they undertake Endeavours.

Each Character engages in a variety of activities called Endeavours and resolves any matters that arise from their choices.

Aside from money gained or saved due to Endeavours, all of the Characters’ money is spent.

Characters are then ready to start their next adventure.

name: Roleplaying Downtime
text:
The Between Adventures part of a game should be quickly resolved at the end of an adventure, or between the GM and each player individually, before the next adventure begins. Events or Endeavours shouldn’t ordinarily turn into small RPG sessions, as this risks over-focusing on the instigating player or derailing the ongoing campaign. If your group loves roleplaying all their Characters’ interactions, focus on the key relationships and spend a minute or two on each. Adding more detail to the NPC who fences stolen goods for them, for example, makes the world come alive more vividly, and makes it feel much more personal for the player if something threatens that NPC as part of a subsequent adventure.

– Leopold Seidel, Proprietor of The Stuck Pig

name: Regional Events Table
text:
The GM should roll once on the Regional Event table to determine what’s going on in the local area during the Characters’ downtime. If there is some important event, local festival or misfortune, or a prominent piece of gossip doing the rounds that will be important to a future adventure, the GM can substitute that instead of rolling.

01–02: Grand Procession Crowds flock to the roadside to watch as a great procession of the faithful, dedicated to a god of the Empire chosen by the GM, winds its way through the region. Warrior priests, wild figures in animal skins, chanting clergy, or solemn mourners accompany the procession, depending on the cult. Characters devoted to the deity being honoured are inspired by the spectacle, and may choose to make a single Test with Advantage during the next adventure.

03–04: Unusual Mercenaries One or more rare mercenaries turn up in a nearby settlement looking for work: a Tilean Duellist of great repute, the so-called Birdmen of Catrazza, unemployed ogres under the command of a halfling captain, or other unlikely bands. The mercenaries will gladly train any Character in any martial Skills or Talents, at a 20% reduction in costs, should the Characters undertake a Training or Unusual Learning Endeavour.

05–07: Auguries of the West Wind The surrounding area suffers from a severe drought. In desperation, the local lord sends for help from the Colleges of Magic in Altdorf, who dispatch a wizard with a mighty Celestial Hurricanum. As the esoteric device scours the local landscape with wind and rain, it not only terrifies the locals, but also draws the Blue Wind of Azyr. All Casting and Channelling Tests involving Azyr during the next adventure gain +1 SL.

08–12: Teacher, Teacher! A travelling tutor sets up shop in the local square, offering to teach any and all in exchange for coin. The GM chooses an Advanced Skill. This Downtime, any Character may use the Training Endeavour to learn that skill, without having to use Consult an Expert to find a teacher.

13–16: The Doktor is In A travelling barber surgeon arrives in the region, driving a wagon packed with medical supplies and a reclining leather chair only lightly stained with blood. Scarce and Rare Herbs and Draughts (page 314) have their Availability improved by one step during this Downtime. They will also happily perform any amputations, tooth extractions, or haircuts for free as a demonstration to draw in coin-laden crowds.

17–21: Artisan Caravan A caravan of dwarfen artisans stops off on its journey between holds, willing to trade superior crafting materials. All Tests taken as part of a Crafting Endeavour during this Downtime benefit from +2 SL.

22–26: Flowing Profit Disruption on major roads due to brigands, beastmen, or whatever threatens the locale drives trade to the waterways. All Riverfolk make an additional 50% from any Income Endeavour pursued during this Downtime.

27–30: Opportunity Saunters Through Passing soldiers, well-heeled merchants, or vacationing nobles pass through the area, and those willing to curry favour reap the benefits. Burgher and Peasant Class Characters make an additional 50% from any Income Endeavour pursued during this Downtime.

31–35: Festivities A celebration is called! The GM decides the nature of the event. Possibilities include a local wedding, a feast of Rhya in thanks for a bountiful harvest, or a public execution! With so many people around, any Gossip Tests made during this downtime benefit from Advantage, while Artists and Entertainers double their money from the Income Endeavour.

36–39: Marvellous Miracle Cures A travelling potion salesman arrives in the region, driving a gaudy wagon bedecked with racks of mysterious liquids in vials, jars, and earthen jugs. Scarce and Rare Herbs and Draughts (page 314) have their Availability improved by one step if bought from the travelling merchant during this Downtime. For each item bought this way, the GM rolls a d10: on a 1 or 2, it is actually a Poison (page 313) of the GM’s choosing.

40–42: Levy A local lord levies warriors to form a regiment in his name. Maybe they are looking to contribute to a wider war effort, assemble a private army for their own purposes, or just keep up appearances through sponsoring a temporary military exercise. Characters from the Warrior Class gain an additional 50% from any Income Endeavours as they assist in training or recruiting villagers. Warriors who undertake the Income Endeavour count as having taken the Combat Training Endeavour.

43–45: Travelling Players A colourful troupe of travelling players arrives, erecting a makeshift stage in the market square and performing tales of heroic deeds, tragic romances, and biting satires of local worthies. The local worthies swiftly have them arrested and ban all public gatherings as seditious. Consult an Expert, Foment Dissent, and The Latest News each require 1 additional Endeavour this Downtime as people become fearful of speaking openly.

46–52: Inclement Weather Particularly bad weather arrives. For the next adventure, all social Skill Tests suffer a penalty of -1 SL (everyone is in a foul mood due to the rain), and food prices increase by 50% due to spoiling of stores.

53–55: Religious Mania A brief but intense period of religious mania breaks out, perhaps due to unexplained celestial phenomena, the preaching of a radical prophet, or a beast born with the sign of one of the gods. Any Pray Tests made during this Downtime benefit from Advantage.

56–59: Power Vacuum A prominent local leader — such as a guildmaster, village elder, or watch captain — is suddenly replaced due to illness, scandal, or looking askance at a passing witch hunter. The local political landscape is a powderkeg as factions vie for power in the wake of the change. Foment Dissent only requires 1 Endeavour, rather than 2, this Downtime.

60–64: New Moon The nights are particularly dark, providing ideal cover for those who work in the shadows. Rogue Characters undertaking the Income Endeavour this Downtime increase the money they earn by 50%.

65–68: False Silver To the horror of the merchants, a run of counterfeit coins plagues the locale. Characters who undertake the Banking Endeavour will lose 20% of money banked, and those undertaking the Income Endeavour similarly reduce any money earned by 20%.

69–73: Tax Collector An unexpected visit by the tax collector (with several soldiers in tow) sweeps through the settlement. Those with legal employment earn 50% less from any Income Endeavours due to harsh taxes, while Rogues and others who operate outside the law earn double the usual amount as opportunities for smuggling and dirty dealing abound.

74–81: Crime Crackdown The Watch is cracking down hard. Rogues can get no funds from the Income Endeavour, and if Rogues undertake a Banking Endeavour, they may only select a high-risk deposit, as legitimate banking houses won’t handle dirty money right now.

82–88: Glorious Weather Particularly sunny weather arrives. For the next adventure, all social Skill Tests suffer a penalty of -1 SL (everyone is in a foul mood due to the heat). Dry roads make trade easier, however, increasing the availability of all non-Exotic goods by one step.

89–91: Local Crop Failure Food becomes exceedingly scarce and many folk suffer terribly. Characters from the Peasant Class cannot undertake the Income Endeavour, and food prices are doubled in the area for the duration of the next adventure.

92–94: Malicious Malady The Washers Guild are hard at work as the Bloody Flux sweeps through town. Each Character must pass an Easy (+4 SL) Endurance Test or contract the Bloody Flux (page 180) on a failure.

95–97: Riots Due to a sudden tax increase, public scandal, or the ravings of a deranged prophet, the common folk are furious at the high and mighty! Characters of the Courtier Class cannot take the Income Endeavour as, no matter how many bodyguards they hire, it isn’t even vaguely safe for them to be abroad on business. Players attempting a Foment Dissent Endeavour benefit from Advantage on any related Tests.

98–00: Under Suspicion The party’s irregular movements or sudden wealth has drawn suspicion. The Characters become acquainted with the local magistrate, and must forfeit one Endeavour either laying low or proving their innocence. Characters in the Rogue class cannot use the Income Endeavour until after their next adventure.

name: Character Events Table
text:
Each player rolls d100 on the Character Events table to determine what’s been happening to their Character during the Downtime. Some Events may impact Endeavours and other Downtime activities, while others have effects that linger for your next adventure.

01–04: Inspiration Strikes Through diligent study or a flash of sudden inspiration, you make a breakthrough at improving your skills. Gain 50 XP.

05–09: Unexpected Esteem Someone you helped in the past has a chance to repay your efforts. The precise nature of the reward should be appropriate to your past deeds, and the NPCs you have assisted during play or in your back story. The tokens of gratitude may vary from a single high-quality item, to a purse of silver (which will be available at the start of the next adventure). Of course, not all gifts are what they appear and the GM may attach an awkward complication to this sudden windfall.

10–14: Somebody Else’s Problem Whether through luck, good timing, or a fortunate misunderstanding, somebody else ends up dealing with a problem that would normally have landed on your doorstep. You find yourself with some unexpectedly free time. Gain 1 additional Endeavour to use this Downtime.

15–19: A Quiet Week Nothing catches fire, the tax collector passes you over, and nobody accuses you of witchcraft. By the standards of the Empire, it has been an extraordinarily peaceful week. During the next adventure, you may ignore the first Fumble or Minor Miscast you would suffer.

20–24: A Good Day’s Work Fortune smiles upon your labours. Perhaps a satisfied customer recommends your services, your master is unusually generous with your wages, or your latest mark was particularly gullible. Should you take the Income Endeavour this Downtime, increase your Standing by 3 for the purposes of determining how much you earn.

25–26: Is that an Original von Klapper? A bespectacled noble passing you on the street suddenly stops and exclaims with excitement. They are convinced that one of your Trappings (determined by the GM) is in fact a rare and important example of a particular artisan’s work. You may immediately sell the Trapping to the hapless collector for twice its listed value.

27–29: Morr’s Embrace A relative, old friend, or mysterious benefactor dies and leaves you some money in their will. Gain some coin appropriate to your Status — Brass: 20 brass pennies; Silver: 10 silver shillings; Gold: 2 gold crowns. This windfall is received before completing Endeavours, so must be spent or banked before jealous family members, opportunistic cutpurses, or hidden burial fees whisk it away; see Money to Burn below.

30–34: Forewarned is Forearmed You are given a cryptic omen by a dream, two-shilling mystic, or Celestial wizard you encounter on the street. During your next adventure, your maximum Fortune points are increased by 1.

35–41: What a Bargain! While browsing the local markets, you come across an item tucked away in a stall that has clearly been overlooked by the merchant, who doesn’t know the value of what they have. You may purchase a single Trapping for half its usual price.

42–47: Pedlar A wizened, well-travelled pedlar who likes to gossip passes through. For the price of a flagon of ale (6 d) you may attempt the Latest News Endeavours without using one of your Endeavours.

48–51: A Useful Connection Through your labours or a social encounter, you find yourself in the home of an accomplished artisan or scholar. Without requiring one of your Endeavours, you may choose one of the following options: undertake the Commission Endeavour, or undertake the Research Lore Endeavour, with Advantage on any associated Tests.

52–56: Soothsayer You discover a small tent in a corner of the local market square, from which wafts the scent of incense and bitter herbs. A wizened crone beckons you inside and offers to read your fortune. For the price of 1 shilling, you may acquire the Doomed Talent, if you do not already have it, or otherwise roll on the table of Doomings (page 118) replacing your previous result with the new result. Should you try to locate the tent again so your companions can get a reading, you are mysteriously unable to find it.

57–59: Arcane Auction The belongings of a recently deceased neighbour are auctioned, including a dusty, old book of unknown origin. If you are able to pay the 2 GC asking price, the book is yours! Beyond any other secrets the book may reveal, as determined by the GM, you (or any other Character of your choice who can read) may undertake the Research Lore Endeavour without using one of your Endeavours, making any required Test with Advantage.

60–67: Oi! You spilled my pint! While carousing in a tavern, browsing the markets, attending a cult rite, or any appropriate activity, you run afoul of a hot- headed member of a local guild, criminal enterprise, or other organisation. The GM determines the faction in question and, during the next adventure, you suffer Disadvantage on social Tests with members of that group.

68–74: Onerous Obligations A family wedding, guild meeting, temple festival, or some other unavoidable obligation demands your attention. By the time every duty has been discharged and every long-winded acquaintance has finished bending your ear, little time remains. You have 1 fewer Endeavour to use this Downtime.

75–79: Impounded A zealous official decides one of your possessions requires inspection, a new licence, or proof of ownership. Recovering it means navigating the Empire’s labyrinthine bureaucracy. Spend 1 Endeavour reclaiming one of your Trappings (chosen by the GM), or begin the next adventure without it.

80–84: Ranald’s Wrath Whether you cheated the wrong gambler or laughed at the wrong joke, the trickster god seems to have taken an interest in you… for the worse. Your clothes catch on each nail you pass, every ale you order is sour, and a pigeon relieves itself on your hat three times in one day. During the next adventure, your maximum Fortune points are decreased by 1.

85–90: Scandalous Rumours Through no fault of your own — or perhaps entirely through your own doing — you become embroiled in a local scandal. Awkward conversations and sidelong glances follow wherever you go. During the next adventure, you cannot spend Fortune on social Tests.

91–92: Betrayed! A friend, family member, or ally turns on you. Decide with the GM who betrayed you and why. During the next adventure, the betrayer or their agents may complicate your plans at least once. Whether or not you can make amends in some way is up to the GM.

93–97: Accused Ally One of your allies (GM’s choice) is implicated in a crime. A Character with a Law Guild Licence can use up one of their Endeavours to defend the ally on a successful Average (+2 SL) Lore (Law) Test. Otherwise, 3 Endeavours spent by the party will exonerate their ally (or, if guilty, concoct a convincing alibi). If the ally is freed, gain a Major Favour (see Do Me a Favour on page 200) for future use. If not, the ally faces punishment — fines, imprisonment, or even execution, as the GM sees fit.

98–00: They’re a Witch! A fearful local or an enemy with ulterior motives accuses you of witchcraft. You may spend an Endeavour and make a Difficult (-1 SL) Charm Test to attempt to clear your name. If you fail the Test or do not attempt to clear your name, a witch hunter takes interest in you. The GM may have them show up at inopportune moments during your adventures until you successfully clear your name. Killing the witch hunter will only confirm people’s suspicions and set their allies upon you.

name: Money To Burn
text: After you’ve rolled on the Character Events Table, you can spend the money earned during your last adventures using the normal rules. After completing your Endeavours, all money held by your Character is considered spent. All of it. The silver lifted from a Burgher’s purse? Gone. The booty liberated from pirates? Also gone. That Troll hoard you raided? Gone, too. All of it. What happened to it? It was spent, stolen, drunk, gambled, used for repairs, to pay off debts or taxes, given as a charitable donations or votive offerings, spent on bribes, or used in whatever other way you prefer. You should concoct the best story for what happens to those funds, as it explains a lot about your Character. If you want to keep some of your hard-won coin to use in the future, you should undertake the Banking Endeavour on page 197. If you want money at the beginning of the next adventure, honestly, or otherwise, depending on your Career, you should undertake the Income Endeavour on page 199.

name: Advance Career
text: To advance in your Career, you need to spend some time rubbing shoulders with the right people, impressing your superiors, or removing those that block your rise with a discreet knife to the back. Once you have filled enough boxes on the Career Advancement Tracker on your Character Sheet by aquiring Trappings, Talents, and Advances, choose this Endeavour and spend 100 XP to move up a level in your Career. You must tick 10 boxes before moving up to level two, 12 more for level three, and 14 more for level four, as shown on your Character Sheet.

name: Burdens of Power
text:
‘The common folk will never understand my burdens. The sheer weight of the duties I bear. The guilty will not judge themselves, and there are always so many villages to cleanse, for our enemies are legion.’

– Hulbart Voggentraas, Witch Hunter

As you climb the ranks of your career, you accrue expectations and responsibilities that cannot be avoided. Noble Lords must see to the affairs of their estates, Guildmasters must oversee their guild’s work, and Watch Captains must watch their watchmen. If you neglect your responsibilities, you will soon lose status amongst your peers.

If you have reached the highest Level of your Career and do not take the Income Endeavour — representing the time spent attending to the demands of your position — you must still make the Earning Test (see Income, page 199). On a success, you do not lose any status, but also do not earn any coin. On a failure, your Standing permanently decreases by 1 within your current Status Tier. Each time you later take the Income Endeavour, your Standing increases by 1, up to the maximum for your current Career Level.

If losing Standing this way would reduce your Standing to 0, you drop a level within your Career; reverting from the fourth level to the third. This costs no Experience Points, acting as a free Career change, albeit downwards.

With this step backwards in your Career Path, you will now have a lower Status, and will earn less money should you perform future Income Endeavours. See Chapter 3: Class and Careers for more about Status. The loss in status does not remove any Advances acquired while you were at the higher Career level.

If you wish to reclaim your lost Career level, you must once again pay the XP cost to re-enter the higher level of your Career and retake your ‘proper’ place in society.

name: Common Endeavours
text: Below you will find details of the Endeavours any Character may undertake between adventures. Note that the GM can decide whether a particular Endeavour is available, given the location and circumstances of the Characters during their period of Downtime.

name: Duties & Responsibilities
text: You may lose one or more of your Endeavours due to your Career or Species.

name: Elves and Yenlui
text:
‘There are times when I can barely stand Altdorf. It is not the stench — though that is abhorrent — it is not the noise, either — it is just that you are all so very ugly to look upon, I feel that I must gaze at something beautiful for a time or I know that I shall start screaming, and never stop.’

– Irlianmaris Ellarel, Asur Envoy

The spiritual philosophy known as yenlui is common to elven cultures. Mastering this discipline is essential for an elf to maintain their soul’s balance between darkness and light. Excess darkness can lead an elf into acts of depravity and cruelty, whereas too much light leads to world-weariness and distraction.

Because of this need to maintain a sense of spiritual and psychological balance, an elf Character must spend one of their Endeavours ensuring that they keep control of their psyches, using at least some of their time away from adventuring to meditate, pray, and attain a state of harmonious yenlui.

The High Elf Players Guide gives more detailed information on maintaining yenlui, and what the consequences are of failing to keep it in balance. If using those rules, the elf Character does not need to spend one of their Endeavours on monitoring yenlui — either they will be keeping it under control as a result of their behaviour, or suffering as a result of being imbalanced.

name: Endeavours
text: Activities Characters undertake between adventures are known as Endeavours. You may choose one Endeavour per week if you are not adventuring, up to a maximum of three Endeavours in each period of downtime.

name: Banking
text:
All the money remaining at the end of your ‘Between Adventures’ phase is lost before the next adventure begins, unless it is saved with this Endeavour. You have two options when taking the Banking Endeavour:

Invest with Banking House Gold and Silver Status Characters only. Determine risk and reward — choose a number between 1 and 10 (or roll 1d10). This is the rate of interest you will accrue, and also how risky the investment is. Withdrawing funds requires another Banking Endeavour, either immediately after the initial Endeavour, or after subsequent adventures. Roll 1d100: if you roll equal to or less than the risk and reward number, the venture has failed and you have lost all of your money. If you roll over the interest rate, you receive your initial funds, plus the interest accrued.

Stash the Loot Hide/bury/give to someone for safekeeping — a high risk option available to all Characters Withdraw money from a stash before the start of an adventure without undertaking an Endeavour. Roll 1d100: if you roll 10 or lower, your stash has been found and you have lost all your money, otherwise you receive your initial funds. If you successfully withdraw your funds they are available for you when you start your next adventure, in addition to any funds secured via an Income Endeavour.

Example: Gerhard and Ulli’s courage in the face of a horde of goblins (not to mention some judicious looting) has earned them a haul worth 10 gold crowns each. The ever-prudent Gerhard decides to place his money with the esteemed Fooger’s Counting House in Marienburg. The GM rolls 1d10 with a result of 6. Gerhard will earn 6% interest on his deposit (12 silver shillings, see page 296), and the investment will fail if he rolls 6 or less on d100 when he tries to make a withdrawal.

Ulli — a gambler at heart — buries his money near a mile- marker on the road to Wrecker’s Point. He doesn’t need to make an Endeavour to get access to his loot, but tragically he rolls 07 when he tries to recover it, and finds nothing but freshly disturbed earth, an empty chest, and a whole heap of regret.

name: Change Career
text: Time spent on this Endeavour represents making the appropriate introductions, doling out bribes, acquiring permits and anything else needed to start a new Career. Work out the particulars with your GM — switching from Soldier to Sailor might be as simple as being press-ganged into the navy, while switching from a Rat Catcher to become a Noble is all but impossible. Additionally, not every Career is available to every Species. Assuming your GM agrees, you may pay 100 XP to change to a Career within your current Class, or 200 XP to change to a Career in another Class.

name: Combat Training
text: You spend time training with the weapons you know, honing your skills for the day when it matters most. After undertaking this Endeavour, you may reroll one Melee or Ranged Skill Test in your next adventure. You can take this Endeavour multiple times if you wish.

name: Commission
text:
So, you wish to own one of von Meinkopt’s legendary repeating pistols, or commission a custom shield with a personalised crest representing your greatest victory? The Commission Endeavour allows you to acquire Exotic Trappings and other bespoke items unavailable in the Empire’s shops. Such commissions take time.

If you wish to commission an Exotic item, you must first find someone capable of making or acquiring it. If you do not already have such a contact, undertake Consult an Expert to locate one. Once you have found a suitable craftsperson or supplier, place your order and pay the item’s cost. It will be ready for collection after your next adventure.

Each Commission Endeavour allows you to order one Exotic item. Additional items require additional Commission Endeavours.

name: Consult an Expert
text:
You may undertake the Consult an Expert Endeavour either to facilitate another Endeavour—such as Commission, Training, or Unusual Learning — or to obtain specific knowledge.

First, you must locate an expert, unless you already know one. Make a Challenging (+0 SL) Gossip Test. On a success, you find a genuine expert. On a failure, you instead find the loudest self-proclaimed authority in the area, and the quality of their advice is up to the GM.

Experts rarely give their time freely. They may require payment, or ask you to perform one or more Favours (see Do Me a Favour!, page 200), which can be called upon during a future adventure or ‘bought off ’ by spending Endeavours between future adventures. The GM determines what, if anything, the expert demands.

The information you receive depends on both the expert consulted and the questions you ask. Academics know the history of their subjects, wizards of the Colleges of Magic understand magic and mystical artefacts — especially those of their own Order — Apothecary Generals can identify even the rarest poisons, and Verenan scholars recall countless historical events. Every expert presents their knowledge through the lens of their own experience and biases.

If you use this Endeavour to gain knowledge, rather than support another Endeavour, you also gain an Expert Reroll (record this on your Character Sheet). You may use this reroll once on a Test directly related to the knowledge you gained before the end of your next adventure.

name: Crafting
text:
Crafting allows you to make any trapping from Chapter 11: Consumer Guide (or anything else the GM allows) if you have the correct Trade Skills. To do this, you require appropriate Trade Tools, raw materials, and access to an appropriate workshop. In general, the raw materials to create the trapping of your choice will cost a quarter of the Trapping’s list price.

To craft the Trapping, attempt an Extended Trade Test, with a Difficulty set by the GM, typically using the Trapping’s Availability as a loose guide.

name: Crafting Difficulty
text:
| Availability | Difficulty |
| --- | --- |
| Common | Average (+2 SL) |
| Scarce | Challenging (+0 SL) |
| Rare | Difficult (-1 SL) |
| Exotic | Very Hard (-3 SL) |

name: Crafting Sl Required
text:
| List Price | SL |
| --- | --- |
| Brass | 5 |
| Silver | 10 |
| Gold | 15+ |

name: Custom Gear
text:
With a GM’s permission, a Character may undertake two (or more) consecutive Commission Endeavours to acquire even more unusual items: personal commissions from the Engineering Guild, a rare and virulent poison, or a magically ensorcelled item. The prices for such things generally range from ‘very high’ to ‘staggering’ and may well involve a Favour or two (see Do Me a Favour! on page 200) or even an entire adventure to acquire raw materials.

The number of SL required to succeed at the Test is also set by the GM, using the listed price for the trapping in the Consumer Guide as a reference.

The SL required is further modified by the Qualities or Flaws you work into the Trapping. Each Flaw halves the SL required, and each Quality adds +5 (worked out after halving for Flaws). Each Endeavour you spend Crafting allows you to make one roll towards your Extended Test. Unfinished work can be kept in whatever you have that amounts to lodgings, or carried around with you as you adventure, should that be possible.

name: Foment Dissent
text:
If you wish to stir civil unrest against a specific individual, group, or institution, undertake the Foment Dissent Endeavour. By spreading rumours, leading meetings, and exploiting local grievances, you gradually turn public opinion against your chosen target. This takes time, requiring two Endeavours (and also counts as an Income Endeavour if you are an Agitator).

First, make an Average (+2 SL) Gossip Test to identify the local power players. If successful, make a Charm Test, with the Difficulty determined by how unpopular the target is. Turning a mob against a hated noble may be Easy (+4 SL), while stirring outrage against a respected Shallyan hospice could be Hard (-2 SL). If either Test fails, the Endeavour fails.

If successful, you can attempt a Charm Test during your next adventure to rally a mob against your chosen target. The GM sets the Difficulty according to the circumstances. On a success, an angry crowd gathers to heckle, threaten, and harass the target. An Impressive or Astounding Success may spark a riot or even an attempted burning. Failure means the crowd refuses to act, while a particularly bad failure may alert the target or their supporters.

Once you have successfully fomented dissent, you may try to turn the mob against a different target during the same adventure, though the Charm Test is two Difficulty levels harder.

name: Earned Income
text:
| Status Tier | Income |
| --- | --- |
| Brass | 2d10 brass pennies per Standing Level |
| Silver | 1d10 silver shillings per Standing Level |
| Gold | 1 gold crown per Standing Level |

On a failure, work is scarce, expenses mount, or some new tax eats into your wages. Roll your earnings as normal, but halve the amount received, rounding down.

Certain results on the Events Tables may directly affect your income. The money you get from an Income Endeavour is given to you after your money from the last adventure is spent (see Money to Burn).

Example: Molli needs to earn some coin, so she takes to the streets to do some good, honest thieving. As a Thief, her Earning Skill is Stealth (Urban), so she makes an Average (+2 SL) Stealth (Urban) Test. Her Stealth (Urban) is 46, but she rolls 83 — a failure even with the +2 SL bonus. Ranald has turned his back on her, it seems. Molli is a Level 1 Prowler with Brass 3 Status, so she rolls 6d10 for her income. The result is 34, halved to 17 because of the failed Test. She earns just 17 brass pennies this Endeavour, and makes a mental note to leave an offering at the next shrine to Ranald in the hope of regaining the Trickster God’s favour.

name: Hardly Working
text:
If you do not take the Income Endeavour during Downtime, you neglect your Career and earn no income. You begin the next adventure with just a single coin appropriate to your Status Tier: 1 brass penny, 1 silver shilling, or 1 gold crown.

For Characters at the highest Level of their Career, neglecting the demands of their position has more lasting consequences. See Burdens of Power, page 196.

name: Income
text:
Most people resume their usual employment between bouts of adventuring. Bounty Hunters hunt bounties, Riverwardens ward rivers, Troll Slayers slay trolls — in the modern Empire, some even rely on a lucrative skill not featured in their job title. Wealthier Characters, such as Nobles and Merchants, might collect a stipend by (briefly) indulging their family, or collecting interest on their investments and business ventures. Roguish types have any number of means to acquire funds, though it’s best not to ask for details.

Take the Income Endeavour to represent your Character working in their chosen Career. Make an Average (+2 SL) Test using the Earning Skill listed in bold italics in the first Level of your Career. On a success, you earn income based on the Status of your current Career Level, as shown below.

name: Invent!
text:
The Invent Endeavour allows you to create entirely new Trappings by combining the properties of two or more existing ones. A pair of Pistols might become a Repeating Pistol, or Pigeons combined with Bombs might produce Pigeon Bombs. The exact effects of any invention are ultimately determined by the GM.

Inventing is a two-stage process: Plan and Build.

Plan: Decide which Trappings you wish to combine, then spend 1 Endeavour creating your blueprints. Make a Trade (Engineer) Test, with the Difficulty determined by the GM according to how ambitious or outlandish the invention is. On a success, the plans are complete. Each SL scored grants +1 SL when you later attempt to Build the invention.

Build: Complete the invention by undertaking either a Crafting or Commission Endeavour.

Crafting: You build the invention yourself. You must possess the Skills required to create each component — for example, combining Pigeons and Bombs requires Animal Training and Trade (Explosives). The Crafting Test is always Very Hard (–3 SL), modified by any bonus gained from the Plan stage. The raw materials cost twice the combined listed price of the Trappings and have an Availability equal to the rarest component.

Commission: You hire someone else to build the invention. You may first need to undertake Consult an Expert to locate a suitable engineer. Resolve the Commission Endeavour as normal, except the work costs six times the combined listed price of the Trappings.

The GM has the final say on the rules and capabilities of every invention.

name: Do Me A Favour!
text:
The powerful often find it preferable to be owed favours rather than money. They are already wealthy, and a favour can be a superior investment: help a student today, call in a favour from a successful Lawyer years later. Favours may be referred to as ‘boons’, ‘services’, or ‘obligations’, but they all amount to the same.

Favours come in three levels: Minor, Major, and Significant. Regardless of a Favour’s level, in almost all cases, the person owed the Favour will take into account the capabilities and sensibilities of the person they’re asking. There’s no point in demanding that a Priestess of Shallya assassinate a merchant, for example, even if she does owe you a Significant Favour. That being said, Favours are ripe for NPCs to exploit in order to put pressure on your moral compass.

A Minor Favour represents a simple task that can be completed in no more than a few hours. Perhaps you need to volunteer at a Shallyan mercy-house or put in a good word for someone. With the GM’s permission, you may undertake an Endeavour to pay off this favour.

A Major Favour is a more time-consuming or risky undertaking. It could take up to several weeks to achieve and may involve travel. Perhaps you are needed to act as lookout on a string of burglaries, convince the Stevedores’ and Teamsters’ Guild to back down from a guild war, or transport a package to a different city. With the GM’s permission, you may undertake two or more consecutive Endeavours to pay off this favour.

A Significant Favour is relatively rare and will almost certainly involve risking life and limb. Months of travel may be involved, and major violence is likely. Perhaps you will be asked to eliminate a rival gang boss, wipe out a goblin encampment, or instigate a riot. Significant Favours cannot be paid off via Endeavours; they are roleplayed out as full adventures.

In the Old World, breaking one’s sworn word carries significant social ramifications. No-one trusts oath breakers, meaning your Status is reduced by 1 Tier (see page @@). Powerful and dangerous folks tend to take it very, very poorly if someone refuses a Favour owed them, so bloody consequences may follow.

name: Research Lore
text:
This Endeavour allows you to seek greater knowledge concerning a specific subject, such as the site of a battle, a famed historical event, or an individual. Your Character must have access to an appropriate storehouse of lore, such as a library, the annals of a dwarf hold, the records of a guild, or a temple of Verena.

Attempt an Average (+2 SL) Research Test. If you succeed, you learn one piece of interesting, useful, or hidden knowledge about the subject researched, and each SL adds another piece of relevant information. If you fail particularly badly (an Impressive or Astounding Failure), you learn something false that you are convinced is true. To facilitate this, the GM may want to make the Research Test in secret on your behalf.

name: The Latest News
text: This Endeavour allows you to learn the latest news from afar. Attempt a Challenging (+0 SL) Gossip Test. On a success, you hear an interesting rumour, with your SL determining how accurate and detailed it is. The news may relate to an upcoming adventure, events elsewhere in the region, or anything else the GM considers appropriate. If you fail particularly badly (an Impressive Failure) you learn something false you are convinced is true. To facilitate this, the GM may want to make the Gossip Test in secret on your behalf.

name: Study a Mark
text:
Use this Endeavour to observe a potential target and gain advantages during future criminal enterprises. A Charlatan may study a merchant in order to better impersonate them during a future scam, or a Thief may spend time watching the comings and goings of a warehouse’s guards to get an idea of their patrol routes.

Attempt a Challenging (+0 SL) Perception Test, though the difficulty may be modified for especially easy or difficult marks. If you succeed, you may gain Advantage on a Test concerning your mark once during your next adventure. Note this on your Character Sheet. You can take this Endeavour multiple times if you wish. Further, the GM should provide information (or disinformation!) concerning your mark according to the SL you scored.

name: Training
text:
This Endeavour allows you to train a Skill or Characteristic outside your Career. In addition to the normal XP cost, you must also pay a tutor. Training in Basic Skills and Characteristics costs a number of pennies equal to the XP cost of the Advance. Advanced Skills cost twice that amount. For more on Advances, see page 191.

You should be able to find a tutor for most skills, especially in a large city such as Altdorf. For some specialist Skills, however, you may first need to undertake Consult an Expert to locate a suitable teacher — those willing to teach Pick Lock, for example, rarely advertise their services.

Some Skills, particularly certain Lore Skills, can only be learned at appropriate institutions, while others are outright forbidden in the Empire. Finding a tutor able (and willing) to teach proscribed subjects, such as Necromancy or those related to the Ruinous Powers, may itself become an adventure. Such tutors usually demand far more than the usual fee, often requiring a Significant Favour (see Do Me a Favour!, page 200).

name: Unusual Learning
text:
It is one thing to pick up a Skill that can be readily practised, quite another to awaken a Talent. This Endeavour allows you to learn the first level of a Talent outside your Career. It cannot be used to gain additional levels in a Talent you already possess.

You must first find a suitable tutor. In most large cities this is straightforward, but particularly obscure Talents, or those sought far from civilisation, may require you to undertake Consult an Expert first. Once you have found a tutor, training costs 4d10 silver shillings.

name: Manann — Penances
text: Penances from Manann often involve hazardous, maritime pilgrimages, tests of sailing skills, or expeditions against the sea god’s enemies, especially followers of the heretical Cult of Stromfels, god of predators.

name: Manann — Strictures
text: No whistling or swearing when at sea or on holy ground. Never harm an albatross. First catch to Manann. A silver and fish to every Manannite temple and shrine approached. Hunt down the servants of Stromfels wherever they may hide.

name: Morr — Penances
text: Morr’s penances typically involve hunting necromancers and destroying undead, or finding and restoring burial places and holy sites fallen to disuse and disrepair. He also occasionally requires servants of Khaine be stopped from fulfilling their dark deeds.

name: Morr — Strictures
text: Respect and protect the dead. Hunt down necromancers and the undead wherever they may gather. Pay heed to your dreams. Never refuse to conduct a funeral service. At no time be a party to raising the dead, unless allowed by Morr.

name: Myrmidia — Penances
text: Penances from Myrmidia are usually military in nature. A cultist may be ordered to defeat an enemy champion in single combat, or to train a group of peasants and lead them in the defence of their village. Protecting pilgrimage routes to sites of importance to Myrmidia are also not uncommon.

name: Myrmidia — Strictures
text: Act with honour and dignity in all matters. Respect prisoners of war, and never kill an enemy who surrenders. Show no mercy to the unrepentant enemies of Humanity. Obey all honourable orders. Preserve the weak from the horrors of war.

name: Ranald — Penances
text: Ranald’s penances usually involve stealing into locked and guarded locations to recover precious items or leave a token. Humiliating oppressors of the poor is also common — perhaps by framing a brutal watch captain for a ludicrous crime, for example, or locking him in his own cells. Ranald often sends favoured and disfavoured cultists alike on a Pilgrimage of Fingers, a set of tasks proving capability and loyalty.

name: Ranald — Strictures
text: One coin in ten belongs to Ranald. Never betray another to the authorities; there is no greater sin than informing. Violence is prohibited except in self-defence. It is better to live free and die than live under oppression. There is no honour among thieves, but there is amongst Ranaldans.

name: Rhya — Penances
text: Rhyan penances may involve replanting devastated areas, helping broken households, and maintaining sacred groves. It is also common to find Rhyans tasked to protect helpless families, which can often put them at odds with local bailiffs and law enforcement.

name: Rhya — Strictures
text: Defend families, children, and crops from all harm. Never feel shame for the flesh Rhya gave you. Life is sacred, do no harm lest another life is in danger. Never judge whom another loves. Interrupt the work of the Prince of Excess wherever it may thirst.

name: Shallya — Penances
text: Penances set by Shallya always involve helping the sick, poor, or downtrodden. A cultist might be sent to a village struck by a plague to tend the sick until the disease has passed. Shallya often tasks her servants to help the wounded at war, or patrol popular pilgrimage routes for those unable to complete their journeys due to ill health.

name: Shallya — Strictures
text: Always render assistance without judgement, based only on a person’s need. Never kill, except in self-defence. Suffer not pestilence, nor those who would spread it. Shallya’s work is never done, so turn not to self-indulgence. Never take up arms; a walking stick and courage will suffice.

name: Sigmar — Penances
text: Sigmarite cultists may be ordered to destroy a cell of Chaos worshippers, or expose a corrupt official who is secretly in league with the Ruinous Powers or a foreign power. It is also common to be tasked with building, or rebuilding, local communities to better promote unity and strength in the Empire.

name: Sigmar — Strictures
text: Obey your orders. Aid dwarf-folk, never do them harm. Promote the unity of the Empire. Bear true allegiance to the imperial throne. Root out orcs and goblins, Chaos worshippers, and foul witches without mercy.

name: Taal — Penances
text: Taal’s penances usually involve clearing diseased or mutated monsters from wild areas, replanting sacred trees, and maintaining groves important to the cult. A cultist might also be ordered to climb a high mountain and leave a stone on a cairn at the top, or clear an obstruction at the top of a waterfall. Whatever the specific task that must be undertaken, Taal’s penances almost always challenge the cultist to survive in the wild.

name: Taal — Strictures
text: Offer a prayer of thanks for every animal taken. Spend a week alone communing with the wilderness every year. Eschew metal armour; clad yourself in the hides of Taal. Rely on your own skill, not the advances of gunpowder or cold technology. Never harm an animal except in self-defence or for food or sacrifice.

name: Ulric — Penances
text: Penances set by Ulric are almost always tests of strength, courage, and martial skill. Slaying a powerful monster, or clearing out a nest of beastmen or outlaws, are typical tasks.

name: Ulric — Strictures
text: Obey your betters. Defend your honour in all matters, and never refuse a challenge. Stand honest and true; outside an ambush, trickery and deception are forbidden. Only wear pelts from wolves killed by weapons crafted of your own hands. Blackpowder weapons are not befitting a follower of Ulric.

name: Verena — Penances
text: Penances set by Verena normally involve the recovery or preservation of knowledge, the righting of an injustice, or the resolution of a dispute. Cultists may also be sent to recover a long-forgotten book of lore, or to mediate in a difficult quarrel. This could be anything from a farmers’ boundary dispute to unpicking the complicated politics of two realms on the brink of war.

name: Verena — Strictures
text: Never refuse to arbitrate a dispute when asked. Always tell the truth without fear or favour. Protect knowledge at all costs. Combat must be a last resort when all alternative routes are fruitless. Never become a tool of injustice or heresy.

name: Wrath of the Gods Table
text:
Whenever you Fumble a Pray Test, or when the units die of a Pray Test is equal or lower than your current Sin Points, roll on the Wrath of the Gods table. The GM may also use it, or pluck results from it, whenever you foolishly insult any of the gods.

When rolling on the Wrath of the Gods table, add +10 to the roll for each Sin Point you have accrued. After rolling and applying the result, reduce your Sin points by 1, to a minimum of 0.

name: Divine Manifestations
text: Blessings are subtle, completely imperceptible to those without the Holy Visions Talent, their manifestation usually indistinguishable to good fortune. In this way, clerics of the Old World without the Bless Talent often appear to be as effective as those with it. By comparison, Miracles are overtly manifest, always accompanied by holy signs and portents, which should reflect the circumstances and relevant deity. For instance, an Ulrican Miracle may be accompanied by a chill wind and the spectral howl of wolves, while those receiving a Miracle of Manann may find themselves drenched in saltwater.

name: Petty Concerns
text: Even gentle Shallya grows irritated when the Blessed abuse their privileges. If the GM wishes, multiple uses of Blessings and Miracles in the same scene, on the same injury, on the same target, or similar can anger the gods, and result in Sin Points, typically ranging from 1 to 3.

name: Prayer Format
text:
The name of the Blessing or Miracle

Range: A range in yards, or marked as ‘Touch’, showing you need to touch your target.

Target: The number of targets affected; it may just be you.

Duration: The duration of the prayer, usually expressed as ‘Instant’ or as a number of Rounds.

The description of what the prayer does.

name: Success Levels
text:
For every +2 SL you score in a Pray Test when attempting a Blessing, you may choose one of the following benefits:

Range: +6 yards Targets: +1 Duration: +6 Rounds

If the Blessing in question has a Duration of ‘Instant’, you may not extend the Duration. You may choose the same option more than once. For instance, if you rolled +4 SL on a Blessing of Healing, you could heal three targets you were touching, two targets up to 6 yards away, or one target up to 12 yards away.

Righteousness Wisdom Wit

name: Success Levels
text: For every 2 Success Levels you achieve in a Miracle Pray Test, you may add additional Range, Targets, or Duration equal to the initial value listed in the Miracle. So, a Miracle with a Range of 50 yards could be increased by an extra +50 yards for every +2 SL scored. Miracles with a Range and Target of ‘You’ may only target the Blessed Priest making the Pray Test, and can never have the Range or Targets increased. Similarly, if the Miracle has a Duration of ‘Instant’, you cannot extend its Duration.

name: Touch Miracles in Combat
text: Certain Miracles require you to touch the target. To touch a creature who does not wish to be touched, make an Opposed Melee (Brawling) or Sleight of Hand/Dodge or Melee Test. If required, reverse the Test to determine Hit Location.

name: Petty Spells
text:
For the few humans blessed — or cursed, depending upon your point of view — with the spark of magic, it generally manifests around puberty, and almost always before 25 summers have passed. The first indications of impending witchery are often little tricks, knacks, cantrips, or similar, showing the wizard-to- be should probably be trained for everyone else’s safety.

For elves, this is just a part of growing up, and those with interest in magic are schooled to develop their burgeoning talents. For humans, assuming they avoid being lynched, it likely means years of training as an apprentice to a wizard from one of the Eight Colleges of Magic, after which they should never use the little tricks they learned when young again. But most do.

As Petty Spells are not formally codified, they have many different names. Players are encouraged to devise their own, more characterful names, reflecting their personality.

name: Arcane Spells
text:
Treat Arcane Spells as extra options for every Lore of Magic, including Witch, Dark, and Chaos Lores. They are counted as Lore Spells in all ways, meaning they get the Lore Attributes of Lore Spells, and can only be learned from and taught to those sharing the same Arcane Magic or Chaos Magic Talent.

How these Spells manifest in practice will depend on the Lore of Magic you use. For instance, a spellcaster using the Lore of Fire’s Drop may cause the object to overheat, while a practitioner of the Lore of Shadows may make it slightly insubstantial, causing the object to literally slip between the target’s fingers.

name: Lore of Death
text:
Lore Attribute: The Purple Wind of Shyish carries with it dry, dusty draughts and the insistent rustling of sand passing through time’s hourglass. Targets afflicted by spells from the Lore of Death are drained of life, enervated, and listless. You may assign 1 Fatigued Condition to any living target affected by a Spell from this Lore. A target may only ever have a single Fatigued Condition gained in this manner at any time.

Ingredients: The bones of sentient creatures feature heavily in Amethyst Magic, as do the trappings of death, including wood or nails from coffins, embalming fluids, hourglasses, silver coins, and grave dirt, all carefully presented or engraved. Purple gemstones, materials, and flowers (particularly roses) are also common.

name: Lore of Fire
text:
Lore Attribute: The Lore of Fire, and the Bright Wind of Aqshy, are anything but subtle. Bright spells are bellowed with fervour and manifest themselves in bombastic fashion, with bright flame and searing heat. You may inflict 1 Ablaze Condition on anyone targeted by Spells from the Lore of Fire unless they also possess the Arcane Magic (Fire) Talent.

Ingredients: Pyromancers use a wide selection of flammable materials as ingredients, which are often immolated as the spell is cast, including coal, oils, fats, and ruddy woods. Trappings immune to fire are also common, such as iron keys, carved sections of fire grate, and small oven stones.

Aqshy’s Aegis CN: 5 Range: You Target: You Duration: Willpower Bonus Rounds

You wrap yourself in a fiery cloak of Aqshy, channelling flame into an aegis. You are completely immune to damage from non-magical fire and ignore any Ablaze Conditions you receive. You receive the Ward 7+ Creature Trait (see page 363) against magical fire attacks, including warpfire and Spells from the Lore of Fire.

name: Lore of Heavens
text:
Lore Attribute: Spells cast from the Lore of Heavens are accompanied by the crackling of lightning and the smell of ozone. Spells that cause Damage ignore Armour Points from metal armour. Further, casting any Celestial Spell gives you a glimpse of the immediate future: gain 1 Fortune Point, which you can use until the start of your next Turn.

Ingredients: Astronomical instruments, charts, lenses, and symbols dominate Celestial Magic, as do ingredients associated with augury, such as animal innards, mirrors, glass balls, and bird tongues. Some wind-based spells use wings and feathers, whereas those involving electricity prefer slivers of carved metal.

name: Lore of Life
text:
Lore Attribute: Spells cast with Ghyran, the Jade Wind, are suffused with life, tending to manifest with a vibrant green light. They are often accompanied by natural phenomena given supernatural qualities. Vines, undergrowth, trees, and rivers all bend to the druid’s will.

Living creatures — those without the Construct, Daemonic, Ethereal, or Undead Creature Traits — targeted by Spells from the Lore of Life have all Bleeding and Fatigued Conditions removed after any other effects have been applied as life magic floods through them. Undead targets suffer additional WPB Wounds, ignoring Toughness Bonus and Armour Points.

Ingredients: Druids use a wide variety of naturally occurring ingredients, ranging from rare seeds and nuts, humours gathered from sentient creatures in the flush of life, uncommon tree saps, fertile loam, spring waters, and a variety of living ingredients, including plants and smaller animals.

name: Mystics
text: The Mystic Career can gain access to the Arcane Magic (Heavens) Talent. Mystics who take that Talent can only take these Spells: Fate’s Fickle Fingers, Starcrossed, The First Portent of Amul, The Second Portent of Amul, The Third Portent of Amul. To gain access to the rest of the Lore of Heavens, they would need to enter a suitable spellcasting Career.

name: Lore of Light
text:
Lore Attribute: Spells sung from the Lore of Light tend to emit dazzling rays of blinding white light or shroud the caster in shimmering waves of radiance You may choose to inflict one Blinded Condition on those targeted by Lore of Light Spells unless they possess the Arcane Magic (Light) Talent. Targets with the Daemonic or Undead Creature Traits also suffer additional IntB Wounds, ignoring Toughness Bonus and Armour Points.

Ingredients: Hierophants of the Lore of Light use many artefacts associated with holiness, supplemented by crystals, glass, pyramidions, and small statues carved with sacred symbols, twisting snakes, and moral tales. White candles, silver carvings, and bleached paper are also common.

name: Lore of Metal
text:
Lore Attribute: The Wind of Chamon is dense, and attaches itself to metallic substances. Spells from this lore are accompanied with golden light and heat and are especially effective against foes wearing metal armour. Spells inflicting Damage ignore Armour Points from metal armour and inflict bonus Damage equal to the number of Armour Points of metal armour being worn on any Hit Location struck. So, if your Spell hit an Arm Location protected by 2 Armour Points of metal armour, it would cause an additional +2 Damage and ignore the Armour Points.

Ingredients: Heavy metals of all types, esoterically inlaid or carved, comprise the majority of ingredients, though many spells also use trappings associated with a forge, including sections of a bellows marked with mathematical formula, inscribed chunks of an anvil, or fragments of a furnace.

name: Lore of Shadows
text:
Lore Attribute: Spells cast from the Lore of Shadows are surreptitious and sly: the Magick may be muttered stealthily. Any protective Spells you cast wreathe you in shadows and billowing smoke, providing +2 SL to Stealth Tests for the duration of the Spell.

Furthermore, all Spells cast from the Lore of Shadows inflicting Damage ignore all non-magical Armour Points.

Ingredients: Anything used to shroud or conceal is used for Grey Magic ingredients, including cosmetics, scents, scarfs, spectacles, mirrors, and wigs. Items drawn from professions steeped in intrigue and wisdom are also common, with diplomatic artefacts, badges of rank, and the ultimate expression of power — a blade — prevalent.

name: Lore of Hedgecraft
text:
Lore Attribute: The Hedgefolk believe their lore is a gift from the gods, referring to their spellcasters as the blessed few. Due to their ancient traditions and ingrained belief, their Spells cannot be cast without ingredients, which are an integral part of their spellcasting process.

Fortunately, the ingredients they use are easily found and prepared on the fringes of settlements. You receive 1 + SL ingredients on a successful Average (+2 SL) Lore (Folklore) Test after 2 hours of work, or you can buy them for 5 brass pennies each.

Ingredients: Hedgefolk use easily sourced local materials prepared to exacting standards using special tools. So, ingredients may include things such as the wings of a dragonfly killed with a silver pin, rods of poplar polished with beeswax on Sonnstill, or bones buried beneath a hedgerow for a winter’s month.

name: Lore of Witchcraft
text:
Ingredients for Witchcraft only reduce Miscast level if you roll 01–40 on a Miscast table (keep the roll if moving down to a new table). They are, however, cheap and readily available: herbs and body parts of small animals for the most part. Ingredients cost a Spell’s CN in brass pennies to purchase. Alternatively, you may spend 2 hours foraging with an Average (+2 SL) Lore (Herbs), Outdoor Survival, or Set Trap Test: a success produces 1 + SL ingredients. The Lore of Witchcraft may be used with Channelling (Dhar) or Channelling (Magick).

Ingredients: Witches use a medley of common herbs and a horrific mixture of animal body parts, often harvested when a creature is still alive. It is not uncommon to find them clutching lizard eyes, dog toes, donkey gizzard, or much, much worse in their bloody hands as they cast their foul magics.

name: Lore of Nurgle
text:
The Lore of Nurgle spreads foul disease and filth, mixing bloated excesses of the Jade and Amethyst Winds with whatever corruption comes to hand, then spewing it everywhere.

Lore Attribute: Targets of Spells from the Lore of Nurgle become susceptible to infection and disease. While a Spell from the Lore of Nurgle is in effect, any target who suffers a Wound must Test to see if it becomes a Festering Wound (see page 180).

name: Lore of Slaanesh
text:
The Lore of Slaanesh revels in torture and excess, all offered to the Prince of Pain and Pleasure for its eternal delight. It is typically wrought by twisting together the Grey, Gold, and Jade Winds into something perverse and exotic.

Lore Attribute: Targets of Spells from the Lore of Slannesh find themselves alive to sensation and temptation. While a Spell from the Lore of Slannesh is in effect, targets suffer -2 SL to resist Animosity, Hatred, and Corruption, but gain +2 SL to resist Fear and Terror.

name: Lore of Tzeentch
text:
Tzeentch is the Master of Magic, Treachery, and Lies. The Lore of Tzeentch epitomises this, as it boasts a multitude of powerful spells focusing upon change, all drawing heavily from the Grey, Gold, Blue, and Bright Winds.

Lore Attribute: Those affected by Spells of the Lore of Tzeentch are riven by the transformative magic of Chaos. They must pass a Corruption Test or gain +1 Corruption Point. Should they pass, they instead gain +1 Fortune Point, which can be used until the end of the encounter. Such are the whims of Tzeentch.

name: Extend Caution
text:
Why are Extended Tests explained here rather than in the Rules chapter? Because they are a tool for the GM to use in particular circumstances. Overused, they can bog down the game and feel anticlimactic. When a significant task needs to feel exciting, a series of repeated dice rolls without tension may fail to deliver.

Extended Tests work best for short, tense situations: you have three Turns to pick this complicated lock before the guard arrives — go! They can also show how much of a larger task the Characters can complete before time runs out, such as repairing a fortress before the orc horde arrives. Avoid using them for adventure climaxes, or when a single Test can resolve the situation just as well.

name: The Gm’S Test Toolkit
text:
There are several components of a Test, all of which are tools for the GM to use in fine-tuning the challenge presented to the Players.

SL Modifiers

These come from the Test’s Difficulty and circumstances, or from a Character’s Talents, equipment, and abilities. The GM determines the Difficulty, and may award up to +1 SL for a particularly clever approach. All SL Modifiers are applied after the dice are rolled.

Advantage and Disadvantage

This ability to reverse the numbers in your roll comes from Momentum (page 167), certain Talents, Spells, and Miracles, and from spending Fortune. The GM should almost never grant Advantage or inflict Disadvantage when the rules do not specifically call for it.

Reroll: A reroll is when you disregard the result of a dice roll, and roll it again. You must use the second result. Some Talents allow you to reroll, as does spending a point of Fortune.

Rolling a Double: Rolling a double means both the tens and the units die roll the same number (11, 22, 33, 44 and so on). This is most often relevant for triggering a Critical or Fumble in combat. It gives the GM the opportunity to introduce dramatic or amusing events for good or ill — feel free to get creative in describing what happens!

name: Awarding XP
text:
The secret to awarding XP is to give enough for Characters to feel they are improving without making advancement seem too easy or too fast. Aim for a noticeable bump while leaving plenty of things for players to save towards.

We recommend awarding around 100 XP per session to each player, based on the group’s achievements.

Surviving the session: 50 XP Saving an important NPC’s life: 10–25 XP Finding important information: 10–25 XP Defeating a significant antagonist: 10–25 XP Achieving minor objectives: 10–25 XP

You can also award bonuses for significant milestones.

Achieving the adventure’s main objective: 25–100 XP Completing a series of linked adventures: 100–200 XP

Finally, consider individual bonuses for players who played their Character in keeping with their Character concept (sometimes to their detriment!), who achieved something spectacular (intentionally or not!), or who made everyone else around the table laugh uncontrollably. Try to spread this one around and avoid simply giving it to a player who dominated the session — remember the quiet players who are playing their Character well.

name: Travelling By Road
text:
| d10 | Encounter |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Roadside Shrine: A shrine to Rhya, Taal, or another deity stands beneath an ancient tree. Someone has recently left flowers, candles, or a small offering of food. |
| 2 | Toll Gate: A pair of bored road wardens collect tolls beneath a faded sign bearing the local noble’s coat of arms. One is asleep in his chair, while the other argues with a farmer in a cart about whether their pigs count as livestock or cargo. |
| 3 | Funeral Procession: A sombre group led by a priest of Morr walks behind a cart carrying a shrouded corpse. The priest leads them in prayer while a raven croaks from a cage affixed to the cart. |
| 4 | Gibbet: A weathered gibbet stands beside the road, its occupant long reduced to a pile of bones. Someone has hung a fresh notice from the post warning travellers about poaching, banditry, or some other crime. |
| 5 | Fellow Travellers: Roll on the Fellow Travellers Table to determine who shares the road. |
| 6 | Roadside Inn: Smoke curls from the chimney a low, ramshackle coaching inn ahead. The smells of cooking food and spilled ale waft from its open door. |
| 7 | Beastman Totem: Antlers, bones, and scraps of hide have been lashed together around a dead tree beside the road. Fresh blood stains the earth beneath, and a crude symbol has been daubed across the trunk. |
| 8 | Marching Troops: A squad of soldiers in the off-white uniform of Reikland marches past, pikes shouldered. Their officer bellows for the Characters to clear the road. |
| 9 | Corpse: A body lies face down in the middle of the road, broken arrow shafts protruding from its back. It has been there for some time and tracks on either side show that travellers have passed it by, paying no heed. |
| 0 | Pyre: A smouldering pyre stands by the side of the road, a burned body lashed to a stake at its centre. A hammer or twin-tailed comet has been roughly carved into the figure’s forehead, the clean lines showing it happened after the burning. |

On the best roads, roadside inns can frequently be found every fifteen to twenty miles or so, which unsurprisingly, is around the distance a human traveller on foot can make each day spent walking at a brisk pace for 7 or 8 hours. Such inns are far more sporadic, or even non-existent, away from the major coaching routes, which means travellers will have to camp alongside the road at night — not a safe prospect at all.

River travel can be easy to secure, but dedicated passenger barges generally only travel between pre-determined docks at specific settlements. Getting off at an unscheduled destination will probably require some fast-talking and a modest bribe. Going almost anywhere else requires either a chartered boat, an expensive prospect, or arranging to travel with a cargo vessel, which will likely take a hefty inducement.

name: Travel Times
text:
As a rule of thumb, a traveller on foot or in a horse-drawn wagon can cover around 15 miles in a day, while a traveller mounted on a horse can manage around 30. Express coaches, which change horses along the route, can cover twice that distance, reaching around 60 miles in a day. A river barge travelling downstream can cover roughly 40 miles; while travelling upstream this distance is reduced to a maximum of 15 miles.

These figures assume good roads and reasonable conditions; poorly maintained roads, bad weather, difficult terrain, or other delays can easily reduce the distance covered. When in doubt, use the quality of the road and the circumstances of the journey to adjust these figures rather than worrying about precise calculations.

name: Travelling By River
text:
| d10 | Encounter |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Drowned Tree: The skeletal branches of a dead tree protrude from the river, festooned with ribbons, bones, and scraps of cloth. Someone has carved a five-tined trident, the symbol of Manann, into its trunk. |
| 2 | Ferry Crossing: A ferry carries peasants, livestock, and a couple of priests across the river. Everyone is packed so tightly that a goat is jostling with one of the priests for room, while the ferryman loudly insists that there is plenty of space |
| 3 | Dead Man’s Boat: An unattended rowboat drifts downstream, turning slowly in the current. Blood stains its sides and a coil of rope trails into the dark water behind it. |
| 4 | Fisherman’s Catch: A fisherman hauls something enormous from the river. He beams proudly until he sees what is thrashing in his net, at which point he hurriedly cuts the rope and watches it disappear below the water. |
| 5 | Fellow Travellers: Roll on the Fellow Travellers Table to determine who shares the river. |
| 6 | Plague Barge: A boat drifts at anchor, its windows shuttered and its deck deserted. A white rope has been strung around it, and a small Shallyan shrine on the riverbank bears fresh candles. |
| 7 | Waterborne Revels: A heavily laden barge comes drifting downstream at an alarming angle, its crew loudly singing a drinking song. Someone has clearly fallen asleep at the tiller, but the boat somehow navigates a bend in the river without mishap. As it passes, a barrel rolls overboard, prompting the drunken crew to cheer. |
| 8 | Abandoned Camp: A pair of upturned rowboats lie on the riverbank next to a makeshift campsite. The tents have been slashed open and belongings are scattered haphazardly around. There is no sign of anybody alive. |
| 9 | Warning Shot: As the river passes through a heavily forested area, an arrow whistles from the trees and sticks into the side of the boat. It may be goblins taking potshots or a wood elf scout letting the Characters know not to attempt to land. |
| 0 | Riverbank Gallows: Three wooden gallows stand on the muddy bank, each occupied by a fresh corpse. A painted sign warns that piracy and smuggling are punishable by death. |

name: Consumer Guide
text:
‘Had this feller in here the other day who expected to just be able to pay for a suit of armour and carry it out the same day. Words didn’t seem to have much impact on him, so I invited him to try on a set of greaves I’ve been working on. After they pinched him black and blue he agreed to put a deposit down and made an appointment to get measured next Marktag.’

The Trappings you receive from your Class and Career (see Chapter 2: Character) are enough to get you started, but you might want more equipment. During Character Creation, additional items can be purchased from the lists in this chapter without restriction. However, once you start to play, the availability of some Trappings is limited, so make sure you buy everything you want and can afford before you begin play.

Amulet: A simple brass badge bearing an embossed design or semi-precious stone.

Cloak: Cloaks protect wearers against the elements.

Coat: Protects wearer against the elements and extreme cold; without a good coat or similar, you will receive penalties to resist cold exposure (see page 170).

Courtly Garb: Nobles’ garb features embellishments such as lace cuffs and collars, excessive high-quality fabric and pointed shoes. Servants also wear courtly garb to banquets and ceremonies, although their surcoats and corsets are less ostentatious than the nobles’ fashions and can therefore be purchased at half price.

Velvet Cloak: Among the nobility, the fashion for cloaks of heavy green velvet is so definitive that to say a person ‘is born to the green velvet’ is to call them an aristocrat. Commoners wearing such items are deemed to be acting above their station.

Hat: Fine quality hats are status symbols in the Empire’s towns and cities. The more flamboyant the hat, the better.

Jewellery: Prices vary by craftsmanship, metal type, and gem value. As a general guideline, common rings without any gemstones cost 10 coins equal to their metal type (i.e. brass, silver or gold) whereas necklaces cost 20 coins of the same metal type.

Sceptre: The highest-ranking legal officials carry sceptres to indicate their status.

Signet Ring: Gold rings with engraved stamps are worn by nobles and guild officials, who use them to imprint heraldry or insignia into sealing wax.

Walking Cane: Polished wooden canes with metal caps are status symbols amongst wealthier townsfolk.

name: Guilders
text: If you have an appropriate guild licence, you can use your special contacts to locate rare items. If you fail an Availability Test when trying to buy an item, you can make a Challenging (+0 SL) Gossip Test to talk with your fellow guilders and see if any of them know where you might find what you need. If you succeed, one of your contacts has a few useful suggestions, and you can reroll the Availability Test.

name: Tools And Kits
text:
The majority of tools count as Improvised Weapons when used in combat, however GMs may rule that heavy or sharp tools (e.g. crowbars and sickles) count as Hand Weapons. Many of the individual tools listed here are included in Trade Tool packages and Workshops, and need not be bought separately.

Animal Trap: Used to catch game (see Foraging on page 152, and Traps on page 136).

Antitoxin Kit: Contains a small knife, herbs, and a jar of leeches. A successful Heal Test with an antitoxin kit removes all Poisoned Conditions. Treatment takes at least two Rounds.

Disguise Kit: Contains enough props for four disguises (e.g. wigs and makeup) and also materials for changing your appearance used by those with the Entertain (Acting) Skill (e.g. wax, fake blood, and prosthetics).

Fish Hooks: Can be used to catch fish (see Foraging on page 152).

Lockpicks: An assortment of small, variously-shaped tools needed to use the Pick Lock Skill without penalty. Being in possession of lockpicks may well raise suspicions in many places.

Manacles: Manacles impose an Entangled Condition with a Strength of 65. Only one attempt to break free from manacles can be made per hour unless appropriate tools are used.

Pole: A long pole used for barging; counts as an Improvised Weapon.

Reading Lens: Glass lenses with handles provide a +2 SL bonus to any tests made to decipher tiny or unintelligible writing. Perception Tests to search for fine details such as secret doors or compartments also receive a +2 SL bonus.

Writing Kit: Contains a quill pen, inkpot, and ink blotter.

Book, Apothecary: Hand-written collections of ingredient descriptions and diagrammed instructions for brewing. Formulas for Digestive Tonics, Healing Draughts, and Vitality Draughts are usually included (see Herbs and Remedies). Advanced texts contain formulas for more exotic draughts.

Book, Art: Plays, poems, and ballads scribbled on loose parchment, art books come in many forms. They also include treatises on perspective, form, and style, often written by famous painters or sculptors, such as Leonardo da Miragliano.

Book, Cryptography: Where individual ciphers and encryption keys can be written on a single page or two, cryptography books are often hand-scribed codices dealing with mathematics, numerology, and polyalphabetic encryption.

Book, Engineer: Most engineering books are press-printed. Engineering is an advanced science in the Empire, thanks largely to the Imperial Engineers’ School in Altdorf and the Dwarf Engineers’ Guild. As a result, many engineering texts are authored, co-authored, or edited by dwarfs.

Book, Law: Laws vary considerably from one region to the next. Cities with printing presses compile legislation in bound volumes, whereas judges in smaller towns often rely on documents handwritten centuries ago. Law books used by travelling lawyers or judges often combine printed and written pages from different towns across the Empire, collated and bound together within the same cover.

Book, Magic: Spell grimoires are usually scribed by wizards, and their covers are often secured with locks. Sometimes grimoires are even protected by magical alarms or wards. Carrying a spell grimoire is punishable as heresy unless the owning wizard is licensed by the Colleges of Magic.

Book, Medicine: Medical texts can either be scribed or press- printed, depending on the authoring physician’s prestige. Illuminations are common, and usually include detailed autopsy drawings and procedural diagrams.

Book, Religion: Religious books come in all forms in the Empire. There is an eager market for the most popular texts, most of which are cheaply produced by printing presses.

Guild Licence: Guild licences are usually printed on single sheets of parchment, stamped with an official seal, and signed by the local guild master. Guild licences are not purchased; instead, they are granted to guild members according to each guild’s traditions and laws.

Legal Document: A simple legal document such as a will, IOU, or letter of intent.

name: Travel Prices
text:
The prices listed here do not include meals, lodging, or fodder, although coaches and passenger boats usually charge for the whole package for longer journeys. Package prices can be worked out by combining travel with food and boarding prices.

On some ferries, lodging is not required, as passengers sleep on the vessel, either on deck or in a private cabin.

Cargo barge travel costs should be individually haggled with barge masters. Often, such passage can be secured for a greatly reduced price, or even for free, if the passenger is willing to work and they know what they are doing.

High-class travel is available and fashionable among the wealthy. It may cost many times the listed price, typically ten times or more. Opulent passenger vessels ply the rivers between the great cities of the Empire, like the famous Emperor Luitpold plying the River Talebec between Altdorf and Talabheim.

All the costs listed here are per mile travelled, and are loose guides only. Faster coaches and barges generally cost twice as much. Slower examples cost as little as half as much. Increase or decrease speed by +/– 1 for faster or slower examples.
